records.text: Effective presentation planning involves selecting language, structure, tone, and content that suit the audience, purpose and form, for example: o in speeches, rhetorical questions (e.g. ‘Have you ever wondered why …?’) can engage the audience, inclusive pronouns (e.g. ‘us’, ‘we’, and ‘our’) help build connection, and cue cards can be used to support delivery o in storytelling, figurative language can layer meaning and build atmosphere, a clear narrative structure supports coherence, and pace, volume, and tone help convey mood and guide audience attention o in podcasts, conversational language (informal, natural-sounding speech that mimics everyday conversation) builds rapport, a planned sequence of segments or topics supports clarity and engagement, and the inclusion of examples, signposting, and analogies helps orient the listener.

records.text: Effective presentation planning involves selecting language, structure, tone, and content that suit the audience, purpose and form, for example: o in speeches, rhetorical questions (e.g. ‘Have you ever wondered why …?’) can engage the audience, inclusive pronouns (e.g. ‘us’, ‘we’, and ‘our’) help build connection, and cue cards can be used to support delivery o in storytelling, figurative language can layer meaning and build atmosphere, a clear narrative structure supports coherence, and pace, volume, and tone help convey mood and guide audience attention o in podcasts, conversational language (informal, natural-sounding speech that mimics everyday conversation) builds rapport, a planned sequence of segments or topics supports clarity and engagement, and the inclusion of examples, signposting, and analogies helps orient the listener.

records.text: Language features (e.g. emotive language, rhetorical questions, inclusive language, statistics), structural features (e.g. a thesis statement, counter-arguments, a conclusion with a call to action), and stylistic features (e.g. assertive tone, direct address) shape how ideas are conveyed and how readers engage with persuasive texts.

records.text: A literary essay is a discipline-specific structured form of writing used to explore and communicate interpretations of a text, drawing on key features of text such as theme, character, language, style, and structure.

records.text: A literary essay follows a clear structure that includes: o an introduction with a clear, concise thesis statement that presents a main argument about the text and provides a focus for the essay o body paragraphs that each develop an idea supported by evidence from the text that is analysed to show how it supports the thesis o a conclusion that summarises the main points discussed in the essay.

records.text: Presenting an individual presentation requires: o understanding their audience and purpose, and tailoring content, style, and tone to suit the context, level of formality, and intended impact o selecting an appropriate oral communication form — such as a seminar, formal speech, podcast, spoken word poetry, or whaikōrero — and understanding how oral traditions, past and present, contribute to meaning-making and audience connection o clear organisation of ideas, including a strong introduction, well-structured body, and compelling conclusion that suits the presentation’s intent o using rhetorical devices, purposeful language choices, and presentation strategies (e.g. rhetorical questions, direct address, analogy, storytelling, hooks, signposting, visual aids) to structure ideas and engage the audience effectively o confident delivery techniques — including tone, pace, volume, gestures, facial expressions, and body language — to support meaning and maintain audience attention o practising their delivery to develop clarity, timing, and confidence.

records.text: Presenting collectively in interactive or responsive formats — such as debates, panel discussions, or collaborative presentations — may also require: o clearly stating and defending a position or viewpoint o providing well-researched and credible evidence to support ideas o anticipating and responding to counter-arguments or alternative perspectives to strengthen their position o using persuasive language and rhetorical devices to respond to others, defend viewpoints, and influence audience thinking o maintaining a respectful and courteous tone that supports open, productive exchange in interactive settings o organising ideas logically and coherently to suit the format and audience.

records.text: Examining features of text across a range of forms, including: o in the novel, explaining how features of text — such as characterisation, plot development, setting, trope, and narrative perspective — work together to shape meaning and create effects o in poetry, explaining how features of text — such as rhythm, figurative language, lineation, sound devices, and imagery — work together to shape meaning and create effects o in the short story, explaining how features of text — such as characterisation, pacing, setting, compressed plot structure, and narrative perspective — work together to shape meaning and create effects o in drama, explaining how features of text — such as dialogue, stage directions, tension, dramatic irony, and conflict — work together to shape meaning and create effects o in film, explaining how features of text — such as narrative progression, cinematography, lighting and sound design, dialogue, and visual storytelling — work together to shape meaning and create effects o in non-fiction, explaining how features of text — such as perspective, tone and register, use of evidence, domain- specific vocabulary, and structure — work together to shape meaning and create effects o in oral presentations, explaining how features of text — such as emotive or persuasive language, tone, structure, gesture, and diction — work together to shape meaning and create effects o in visual images, explaining how features of text — such as composition, framing, colour, message, and symbolism — work together to shape meaning and create effects o in media and digital texts, explaining how features — such as tone, visuals, structure, narrative framing, and clickbait — work together to shape meaning, influence perception, and position audiences

records.text: Reading purpose influences response (e.g. a text read for pleasure may inspire emotional, imaginative, or personal responses, whilst a text read for analysis may require structured, critical, or comparative responses).

records.text: Response to text can be developed individually and collaboratively, where discussion — such as in book clubs or reading groups — supports the development, reconsideration, and refinement of ideas through engagement with multiple perspectives.

records.text: Considering an audience involves analysing its characteristics (e.g. age, interests, background knowledge) and anticipating its expectations, which informs decisions about tone, content, structure, and mode of delivery.

records.text: Clarifying purpose means recognising the communicative intention of a text (e.g. to argue a position, analyse a literary text, narrate an experience) and making deliberate choices about structure, language, and style that suit the form and disciplinary context.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 56

records.text: Text conventions vary across forms, modes and disciplines, and writers use specific combinations of language, structure, and style to engage their audience and achieve their intended purpose.

records.text: Planning strategies (e.g. brainstorming, outlining, storyboarding, flow charts) can be purposefully selected and adapted to enhance clarity and coherence, depending on the form and purpose of the writing.

records.text: Writers use feedback to evaluate and refine how effectively a text engages its audience and achieves its intended purpose.

records.text: Discursive texts explore, discuss, or reflect on ideas and viewpoints, often presenting multiple perspectives rather than arguing for a single, specific position.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 56

records.text: Discursive texts can be crafted to achieve different communicative purposes, such as: o to analyse — examining ideas, issues, or texts critically, often presenting evidence and reasoning from multiple angles o to reflect — exploring personal thoughts, experiences, or responses to ideas or events o to explore — considering a topic or question in an open-ended way, without necessarily reaching a conclusion o to speculate — imagining possible outcomes, implications, or interpretations, often using hypothetical reasoning.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 56

records.text: Language features (e.g. rhetorical questions, modality, comparisons, cohesive devices), structural features (e.g. thesis or opening statement, topic sentences, paragraphing that builds or contrasts ideas, transitions between viewpoints, a reflective or synthesising conclusion), and stylistic features (e.g. balanced tone, precise vocabulary, varied sentence structures) shape how ideas are conveyed and how readers engage with discursive texts.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 56

records.text: Persuasive texts aim to convince the reader to agree with a particular point of view, take an action, or adopt a certain belief; they use a combination of emotional appeal (pathos), logical reasoning (logos), and credible evidence (ethos).
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 56

records.text: Persuasive texts are crafted for specific audiences and contexts, and may vary in tone, formality, and structure depending on the medium (e.g. speech, editorial, advertisement).
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 56

records.text: Language features (e.g. emotive language, rhetorical questions, inclusive language, statistics), structural features (e.g. a thesis statement, counter-arguments, a conclusion with a call to action), and stylistic features (e.g. assertive tone, direct address) shape how ideas are conveyed and how readers engage with persuasive texts.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 56

records.text: Creative texts explore ideas, emotions, and experiences in imaginative ways; they often use figurative language, symbolism, tropes, and other literary devices to engage the reader’s senses and emotions.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 56

records.text: Creative texts can use a range of narrative techniques — including flashbacks, foreshadowing, and shifts in perspective or time — to structure and sequence events effectively.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 56

records.text: Language features (e.g. sensory details, metaphors, emotive language), structural features (e.g. metre, varied sentence structures, conflict and resolution), and stylistic features (e.g. tone, diction) shape how ideas are conveyed and how readers engage with creative texts.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 56

records.text: Visual texts communicate ideas, emotions, and messages through design elements to convey meaning; they are designed for specific purposes (to entertain, inform, or persuade) and can take various forms, some of which, (including moving images) will incorporate oral language.

records.text: A literary essay is a discipline-specific structured form of writing used to explore and communicate interpretations of a text, drawing on key features of text such as theme, character, language, style, and structure.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 57

records.text: A literary essay follows a clear structure that includes: o an introduction with a clear, concise thesis statement that presents a main argument about the text and provides a focus for the essay o body paragraphs that each develop an idea supported by evidence from the text that is analysed to show how it supports the thesis o a conclusion that summarises the main points discussed in the essay.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 57

records.text: Accurate grammar is essential for creating clear, structured, and effective communication
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 57

records.text: Accurate grammar includes the correct use of: o clauses o tenses o different sentence types, including simple, compound, complex, and compound-complex sentences o active and passive voice.

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 57

records.text: Accurate punctuation provides clarity in writing and can be used to help readers navigate text smoothly, emphasise key ideas, and control pacing.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 57

records.text: Accurate punctuation includes the correct use of: o apostrophes for showing ownership and contractions o commas for lists and other purposes o colons for lists and explanations o semicolons to link related sentences o quotation marks for dialogue and titles o parentheses o dashes o hyphens.

records.text: Effective vocabulary choices support writers to convey their intended meaning and tone.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 57

records.text: Effective vocabulary choices include the correct use of: o synonyms and antonyms to avoid repetition or to provide the appropriate level of formality for the purpose and audience of their writing o common idiomatic expressions.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 57

records.text: Words have specific connotations, and selecting words with these connotations allows writers to subtly influence a reader’s emotions, perceptions, and interpretations.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 57

records.text: Developing a thesis statement that presents a clear argument about the text, linking multiple features such as theme, character, or authorial technique

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 57

records.text: Structuring body paragraphs to build a cohesive argument, using evidence from the text and analysing it in depth to support the thesis

records.text: Refining their use of advanced punctuation techniques, including ellipses, brackets, and the Oxford comma, to improve the clarity, precision, and style of their texts
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 57

records.text: Presentations take many different forms and are crafted for different purposes, including to inform, to entertain, and to persuade.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 58

records.text: Presenting an individual presentation requires: o understanding their audience and purpose, and tailoring content, style, and tone to suit the context, level of formality, and intended impact o selecting an appropriate oral communication form — such as a seminar, formal speech, podcast, spoken word poetry, or whaikōrero — and understanding how oral traditions, past and present, contribute to meaning-making and audience connection o clear organisation of ideas, including a strong introduction, well-structured body, and compelling conclusion that suits the presentation’s intent o using rhetorical devices, purposeful language choices, and presentation strategies (e.g. rhetorical questions, direct address, analogy, storytelling, hooks, signposting, visual aids) to structure ideas and engage the audience effectively o confident delivery techniques — including tone, pace, volume, gestures, facial expressions, and body language — to support meaning and maintain audience attention o practising their delivery to develop clarity, timing, and confidence.
records.subject: English
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 58

records.text: Presenting collectively in interactive or responsive formats — such as debates, panel discussions, or collaborative presentations — may also require: o clearly stating and defending a position or viewpoint o providing well-researched and credible evidence to support ideas o anticipating and responding to counter-arguments or alternative perspectives to strengthen their position o using persuasive language and rhetorical devices to respond to others, defend viewpoints, and influence audience thinking o maintaining a respectful and courteous tone that supports open, productive exchange in interactive settings o organising ideas logically and coherently to suit the format and audience.
records.subject: English

records.text: Oral communication in New Zealand can be shaped by rich spoken traditions, such as mihi, pepeha, kōrero tuku iho, and whaikōrero.

records.text: Using spoken forms specific to New Zealand supports meaningful communication and respectful engagement when presenting to different audiences, when appropriate to the context.

records.text: Active listening involves questioning (e.g. open-ended questions, paraphrasing, asking for elaboration) for the purposes of clarifying and summarising, and promoting collaborative thinking by inviting others to extend, refine, or respond to ideas.

records.text: Critical listening involves questioning (e.g. Socratic questioning, probing questions) for the purposes of assessing the validity of a spoken text and identifying bias.

records.text: Listening across different genres and contexts requires recognising how purpose, audience, and form shape and enhance meaning.

records.text: Listening to oral traditions and culturally significant forms involves attending to language, rhythm, and delivery to understand meaning and intent.

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 58

records.text: Recognising the structure and purpose of spoken forms specific to New Zealand (e.g. mihi, pepeha, whaikōrero) supports active listening and understanding.
records.subject: English

records.text: Communicating clearly and expressively, adopting deliberate shifts in tone, pace, and volume according to their purpose and audience

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — English Years 0–10, 2025 statement; supplied October 2025 PDF, Year 10, page 58

records.text: External factors like whānau expectations or major life changes can challenge relationships. Managing these pressures is essential to maintain clear communication and healthy boundaries. In addition to effective communication skills, this may include: clarifying values and focusing on what is important within o the relationship having empathy but not owning other people’s problems o respecting differences and that it is okay to disagree o accepting that mistakes or misunderstandings happen o being open and honest about relationship barriers such as o the fear of being judged, ignored, or misunderstood.

records.text: Informed consent is required for organisational data management and all medical treatments. In New Zealand, a person aged 16 or over consents for themselves. records.text: In New Zealand, the legal age of consent for sexual activity is 16 years. Sexual activity with people below this age is unlawful under statutory provisions designed to protect young people from harm and exploitation.

records.text: There are a range of sexual activities in which consenting people experience and express their sexuality. These activities include different forms of physical contact and interaction for sexual pleasure, reproduction, or both.

records.text: Harmful sexual behaviours, like sharing unconsented intimate images or unsolicited attention, severely impact well-being and carry legal consequences. records.text: Stressors (factors causing stress) include personal factors (e.g. poor personal organisation, poor decision-making), interpersonal factors (e.g. others’ expectations), and wider community or world factors (e.g. environmental concerns, overseas conflict).

records.text: Cyberbullying and harmful online behaviours damage mental and social well-being. records.text: Factors reducing online harm vulnerability include digital literacy, using privacy settings, limiting screen time, and acting immediately during incidents. records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Health and Physical Education Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 26

records.text: In New Zealand, cyberbullying is addressed by the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015, which makes it an offence to send or post material with the intention of causing serious emotional distress.

records.text: Chinese calligraphy is a deeply traditional Chinese art form which is commonly used in festive decorations. Messages and blessings are often handwritten to express wishes for prosperity, happiness, and good fortune.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Each Chinese character is written in a square and represents one syllable and a single unit of meaning.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Words in Chinese may be formed from a single character or multiple characters, with each character contributing to the word’s overall meaning.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Strokes, stroke order, and character structure are important features of learning to write characters.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Identify how character structure, position, and component sequences relate to the form and meaning of a character in the Chinese writing system.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 1 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: When greeting someone formally or respectfully, it is common to place the person’s title, rank, or surname first, followed by the greeting.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: There are different greetings and farewells depending on context (e.g. formal, informal, time of day). For example: 您好 (nín hǎo) is a polite form of greeting when greeting seniors, teachers, or o people in higher positions 再 (zài jiàn) is a standard farewell, but 拜拜 (bái bái) is a casual borrowing from o 见 the English ‘bye-bye’ 你好 (nǐ hǎo) has two syllables, and each part carries its own meaning (你 nǐ o (you), 好 hǎo (good, well)). When put together, it literally means ‘you good’.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Greetings, expressions of politeness, and self-introductions often follow cultural norms, including respectful language and gestures such as a slight nod or handshake (depending on the context).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Chinese people usually say their family name before their given name, reflecting cultural values of family and collectivism and showing respect to ancestors.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: When meeting someone new, Chinese people often introduce themselves with their full name.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The pronoun ‘tā’ sounds the same when referring to ‘he’, ‘she’, and ‘it’ and is only distinguished by context. However, in writing, each form is represented by a different character: 他 (he), 她 (she), and 它 (it).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: 马马虎虎 (mǎmǎhūhū), literally meaning ‘horse, horse, tiger, tiger’, is an idiom used to mean ‘so-so’ or ‘okay’, depending on context.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: 呢 (ne) is used after a noun or pronoun to ask about someone or something just mentioned and continue the conversation.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: When reflecting the hierarchical nature of Chinese family culture, individuals traditionally refer to family members by their generational and relational titles rather than using personal names (e.g. 大哥 (dà gē) for eldest brother or二姐 (èr jiě) for second sister).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: 谁, meaning ‘who’, can be pronounced ‘shuí’ (original pronunciation, older and more formal) or ‘shéi’ (more common in everyday speech).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Personal pronouns are foundational elements of communication: 我 (wǒ) o 你 (nǐ) o 他 (tā) o
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Use greetings and farewells for a range of different contexts.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 1 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Introduce oneself and others, and respond to introductions appropriately.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Communicate about family members.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 1 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The words for Monday to Saturday are expressed as 星期 (xīngqī) (day of the week) plus the corresponding number from one to six.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Sunday is either 星期天 (xīngqī tiān) or 星期日 (xīngqī rì).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The names of months are expressed as the corresponding number, from 1 to 12, plus 月 (yuè) (month).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Understanding a person’s age is often essential in Chinese culture, as it helps determine the appropriate form of address and reflects respect for social hierarchy and seniority.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: There are unique hand gestures to represent numbers from 1 to 10 in Chinese culture.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: In Chinese culture, numbers carry deep symbolic meanings that influence daily life, communication, and social customs.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: In Chinese culture, questions about age are treated with politeness and cultural sensitivity. More formal language is used when asking age-related questions of adults and teenagers than of children.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: In Chinese, 岁 (suì) must be used when talking about how old someone is. It cannot be omitted like in English.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The verb 是 (shì) is not needed when saying age (我八岁 (wǒ bā suì)).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Chinese two-digit numbers are formed similarly to te reo Māori, particularly in their logical structure and use of base numbers (1–10) and place values.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Numbers are written by combining characters that show place value: 十一 (11) means ‘ten-one’ o 三十 (30) means ‘three-ten’. o
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: 一 is usually pronounced as ‘yi’, but in some contexts, especially strings of numbers read aloud (e.g. phone numbers, room numbers, zip codes), it is pronounced as ‘yāo’ to avoid confusion with similar-sounding numbers.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Communicate about the days of the week and months of the year.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Communicate about age of self and others.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Colours hold cultural significance in Chinese culture (e.g. red symbolises happiness and good luck and is strongly associated with celebrations like Chinese New Year).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: 吗 (ma) is a particle added at the end of a sentence to form yes or no questions.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: 什么 (shénme) usually comes after a verb but can also appear before a noun when asking for a specific category, such as in 什么颜色? (shénme yǎnsè).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: 不 (bù) (not, no) is placed after a verb to express negation.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: 和 (hé) is a conjunction linking nouns/noun phrases. It cannot link sentences.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Communication can be supported with set expressions for clarification, checking for understanding, asking for repetition, and asking for vocabulary translations.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: It is common for a Chinese-speaking classroom to use a set of formulaic expressions. These expressions are deeply embedded in the everyday routines and interactions of both students and teachers.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: There are several ways to say ‘yes’ in Chinese, depending on context, tone, and formality. 好 hǎo is the most basic and commonly used form.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Communicate about likes and dislikes, including colours, things, and food.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 1 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Understand and respond to simple classroom language, politeness conventions, and formulaic expressions.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 1 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Some initials, finals, and retroflex sounds (which involve curling the tongue back) have more challenging spelling and pronunciation conventions.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Tone changes in Chinese Mandarin follow specific rules to maintain the natural flow of speech.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: There is a commonly recognised four-tone system in Chinese. However, the neutral or silent tone also appears frequently in spoken Chinese. This is especially common when duplicated characters form a phrase, with the second character often pronounced in a neutral tone. For example, 姐姐 is pronounced ‘jiě jie’, with the second character taking a neutral or silent tone.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: It is possible to type pinyin using a standard keyboard.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Because each Chinese character has a unique meaning, idioms which communicate meaningful messages can be formed with as few as four characters.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Stroke order refers to the correct sequence of writing strokes in Chinese characters.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Chinese characters have different structural layouts, such as top–bottom, left–right, and inside–outside.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Components of a Chinese character often provide clues about its meaning (e.g. the radicals 女 (nǚ) and 人 (rén) suggest gender in the characters 她 (tā) and 他 (tā) even though both are pronounced the same).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: People tend to signify respect to seniors or those in authority by making less direct eye contact when communicating with them.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Family friends and elders are addressed using kinship terms like ‘uncle’ and ‘aunty’ to show respect and social hierarchy.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: People are also usually addressed by their surname and a respectful title to show politeness and acknowledge relationships, age, and social roles, especially when speaking to family members, elders, or professionals.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: ‘[title] + 好 (hǎo)!’ is a polite and respectful way to greet people.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: 是 (shì) is equivalent to the English verb ‘to be’. It links a subject to the noun or noun phrase. The negative form is 不是 (bú shì).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: A personal pronoun plus 们 (men) forms a plural pronoun:
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Read, spell, and produce Chinese words, simple expressions, and formulaic phrases in pinyin.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Imitate the pronunciation, stress, intonation, and rhythm in common expressions and simple sentences.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Recognise and use tone symbols and intonation.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Identify and distinguish between similar-sounding phonemes and words in pinyin.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Recognise and write basic components and words in characters.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 2 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Use greetings and farewells in formal contexts.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 2 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Use terms of address and honorific forms.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 2 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: 老师 (lǎoshī) o 老师们 (lǎoshī men). o
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: 叔叔 (shūshu) and 阿姨 (āyí) are used to address parents’ friends.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: 哥哥 (gēge) and 姐姐 (jiějie) are used to communicate with older cousins and friends of older siblings.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: In modern Chinese societies, kinship concepts can be used beyond their literal and familial meanings, including a wider group of close family friends, acquaintances, or even respectful strangers. Examples include: 哥哥 (gēge) o 姐姐 (jiějie) o 叔叔 (shūshu) o 阿姨 (āyí). o
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: In Chinese culture and communities, there are distinct titles for nearly every family member, reflecting a traditionally hierarchical system.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Family plays a central role in Chinese culture. There is a strong sense of duty and responsibility towards one’s family.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Family reunion is a central theme in many traditional Chinese festivals (e.g. Chinese New Year).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Family is a deeply held value across many cultures, and Chinese culture is similar to the concept of whānau in te ao Māori, which reflects strong kinship and community ties.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Repeating syllables in Chinese is a natural and common way to express closeness or affection (e.g. family members and nicknames).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Chinese (Mandarin) has a set of basic pronouns used to refer to people or things, helping to avoid repetition in speech and writing.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Unlike in English, question words in Mandarin Chinese are not placed at the beginning of a sentence. Instead, they usually appear in the same position as the information they replace, often in the middle or at the end of the sentence.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: 有 (yǒu) indicates possession and existence of something (e.g. ‘there is’ or ‘there are’).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: 谁 (shéi/shuí) is a question word used to ask about a person.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: 几 (jǐ) is a question word used to ask about numbers or quantity.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: In Mandarin Chinese, measure words (also known as counters) are used when counting or referring to nouns.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Communicate about family members in more detail.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 2 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Different counters are used depending on the category (e.g. objects, people, family members, animals): 个 (ge) is the basic counter for almost everything o 口 (kǒu) is the counter for family members o 只 (zhī) is the most commonly used counting word for most animals, except fish o and horses.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: 两 (liǎng) is used before measure words and nouns and in time and quantity expressions.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: Chinese people follow a traditional age-counting system known as 虚岁 (xū suì), or nominal age. A person is considered one year old at birth because time in the womb is acknowledged.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: Asking about someone’s zodiac sign can be an indirect and culturally appropriate way to learn their age.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: The Chinese zodiac is closely associated with Chinese New Year, and there are many traditional stories linked to it.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: Use 是(shì) to express time using [subject] + 是+ [time detail].
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: When stating dates in Chinese, the order follows a logical pattern from the largest unit (month) to the smallest (day of the week).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: In oral language, 号 (hào) is commonly used in dates or numbers (e.g. 四月五号 (sì yuè wǔ hào)).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: Telling time in Chinese follows similar logic to dates. It follows from the larger unit (hour) to the smaller unit (minute).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: 半 (bàn) and 刻 (kè) indicate different portions of an hour, as in English. When using them, it is not always necessary to add 分 (fēn).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: The basic word order of a sentence is subject + verb + object (SVO).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: Time markers can be added directly after the subject or sometimes beforehand.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: Communicate about dates and birthdates.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 2 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: Communicate about time.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: Communicate about activities and desires in the here and now.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: In Chinese culture, expressing strong dislikes directly can be considered impolite.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 2 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 15

records.text: Expressing preferences and rejecting others is done politely.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 2 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 15

records.text: Use adverbs and superlatives (the highest degree of something) to indicate different levels of preference.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 15

records.text: Degree words (e.g. very, little) are placed before the word 喜欢 (xǐhuan) (like) to express different levels of preference.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 15

records.text: 要 (yào) (want) is a verb commonly used to express wants or basic needs.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 15

records.text: For polite requests, people often use 想 (xiǎng) or 想要 (xiǎng yào) together instead of 要 (yào) on its own, as 要 (yào) can sound too direct or demanding.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 15

records.text: There are different ways to ask and answer a yes/no question, depending on the context. The most commonly used terms are 对 (duì), 好 (hǎo), and 是 (shì).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 15

records.text: Express preferences about people, animals, or things.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 2 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 15

records.text: Use a range of formulaic expressions to support interactions.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 15

records.text: New vocabulary in Chinese is often built by combining familiar characters with clear meanings, such as: 老人 (lǎo rén) o 小狗 (xiǎo gǒu) o 黑猫 (hēi māo). o
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: The literal translation of 很 (hěn) is ‘very’. However, when used in the basic sentence structure [subject] + 很 + [adjective], it instead often functions as a grammatical connector. It is not used in a negative sentence (e.g.他不聪明（tā bù cōng míng)).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Descriptive words or adjectives are used before a noun. Adjectives can be attributed to a noun or noun phrase by using 的 (de), as in 漂亮的老师 (piào liang de lǎo shī).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Unlike in English, 是 (shì) cannot be used to link a subject to an adjective.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Demonstrative pronouns 这 (zhè) and 那 (nà) are used with counters for stationery, animals, and people. For demonstrative plural pronouns, 这些 (zhè xiē) and 那些 (nà xiē) are used.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: 大 (dà) and 小 (xiǎo) can also refer to age or maturity, not just size.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: 老 (lǎo) literally means ‘old’, but it can also imply experience or seniority, as in 老师 (lǎoshī).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: In spoken Chinese 这一个 is often pronounced ‘zhèi ge’ instead of ‘zhè yí ge’.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: 那一个 is commonly pronounced ‘nèi ge’ instead of ‘nà yí ge’.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Different types of language resources and tools can be utilised for productive, receptive, and interactive skills (e.g. spellcheck, chatbots, and online dictionaries).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: The Chinese concept of time and space is ‘vertical’. The word 下 (down) can be used to express ‘next’ or ‘forward’, whereas 上 (up) can be used to express ‘previous’.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 3 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Time phrases are often used in Chinese to express tense. They are usually placed at the beginning of a sentence but can also follow the subject. However, the verb in Chinese stays the same. They are often grouped together in the sentence.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: 昨 (zuó) is only used for days, whereas 去 (qù) is used for years. For example: 昨天 (zuótiān) o 去年 (qù nían). o
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Communicate using time phrases/markers.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 3 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: In Chinese culture, people prefer to stay warm and not be in the cold. Being cold is often associated with the cause of sickness.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 3 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: The sentence structures ‘[day] + 是 (shì) + [weather]’ and ‘[day] + 天气 + [degree] + [describing words]’ can be used to describe the weather.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: 了 (le) is used to indicate that an action is complete. It is added after the verb. A time word or phrase (e.g. yesterday) can be added to show when it happened, adding emphasis or specificity.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: While 不 (bù) is the basic word for negation, 没 (méi) and 没有 (méiyǒu) are used to say something did not happen in the past.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: In China, school days are often longer, especially in high school. Homework load is heavy, and many students attend after-school classes.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 3 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: Discipline and respect are highly valued in the classroom.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 3 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: Adverbial phrases are used to express details (e.g. time, place, manner) of an action and to sequence ideas, usually preceding the verb or adjective they modify.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: In Chinese, word order is important. For example, frequency adverbs typically come before the action.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: 在 (zài) is one of the basic Chinese prepositions used to show the location of people or objects.不在 (bùzài) is used for negation.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: There are regional differences in vocabulary (e.g. 哪儿 (nǎr) and 哪里 (nǎlǐ) both mean ‘where’).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: 正在 (zhèngzài) can be used to emphasise and express an ongoing action.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: 跟 (gēn) is used to talk about who a person did something with. It can often be used interchangeably with 和 (hé), both meaning ‘with’ or ‘together’.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: Chinese people express politeness through using indirect language, soft particles, and respectful phrasing.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: Polite phrases are used in Chinese to soften requests and commands, reflecting the indirect nature of Chinese. For example: 麻烦你 帮我一下吧 (máfán nǐ bàng wǒ yí xià ba) o 老师不好意思， 我可以去喝水吗? (lǎoshī bùhǎoyìsi, wǒ kéyǐ qù hē shuǐ ma) o 说中文吧 (shuō zhōngwén ba). o
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: 请给我 (qǐng gěi wǒ) is often used with a counter and object (e.g. 请给我可乐 (qǐng gěi wǒ kě lè)).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: Communicate about the weather.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 3 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: Communicate about events and activities that have happened in the past.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: Communicate about habits, hobbies, and daily routines.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 3 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: Communicate about basic commands and polite requests.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 3 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 17

records.text: Chinese culture places high value on modesty and indirectness, especially when it comes to praise. Compliments are often downplayed or deflected to maintain social harmony and avoid appearing boastful.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: 觉得 (juéde) is used to show personal thoughts or reactions (e.g. to think, to feel).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: 想 (xiǎng) is used to express thoughts, opinions, or mental activity.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: 因为 (yīnwèi) is a basic word used to give a simple reason in Chinese.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: Degree words are used to show the intensity or extent of a quality, state, or action (how much or how strong something is). For example: 有点 (yǒu diǎn) o 非常 (fēi cháng) o 最 (zuì) o 太 … 了 (tài … le). o
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: The word 也 (yě) in Chinese means ‘also’ or ‘too’, and it is used to express similarity or addition in a sentence. 也 (yě) comes before the verb.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: Formulaic expressions can be used to facilitate and sustain conversations and real- world interactions, including clarification strategies such as 请再说一遍 or 请再说 一次 (qǐng zài shuō yí biàn, qǐng zài shuō yí cì).
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: Questions such as 你怎么看? (nǐ zěnme kàn) can be used to elicit an opinion.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: Express a basic opinion, providing simple reasons where appropriate.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.section: Novice 3 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: Communicate using an extended repertoire of formulaic expressions, instructions, and short interactions.
records.subject: Chinese (Mandarin)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Chinese (Mandarin) Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18
