records.text: French is an official language in 29 countries.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Greetings and farewell expressions are often accompanied by gestures such as a handshake or a kiss on the cheek, which varies across the countries where French is spoken.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Classroom instructions change depending on whether a single person or a group is being addressed.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: The phrase ‘s’il te plaît’ is used to mean ‘please’ for someone you know well and when talking to one person.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: The phrase ‘s’il vous plaît’ is used to mean ‘please’ when you don’t know the person, they are in a position of authority, or you are talking to several people.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Using the informal ‘s’il te plaît’ when you should use ‘s’il vous plaît’ could be interpreted as rude.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Formal titles of address such as ‘Monsieur’ and ‘Madame’ are commonly used in French and as part of everyday greetings.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Communication can be supported with set expressions for clarification, checking for understanding, asking for repetition, and asking for vocabulary translations.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Respond to and use simple classroom language and politeness conventions.
records.subject: French
records.section: Novice 1 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Recognise the words for common classroom objects and expressions of location.
records.subject: French
records.section: Novice 1 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: French is not the only language spoken in France. There are also regional languages and dialects across the country.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: France has overseas territories and departments throughout the world. New Caledonia, which is an overseas territory of France, is the closest geographical neighbour of New Zealand.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: From 17 onwards, numbers follow the same pattern where the tens unit is followed by the ones unit. In writing, there is a hyphen (-) between each place value (e.g. ‘dix’ + ‘sept’ for ‘dix-sept’, ‘vingt’ + ‘deux’ for ‘vingt-deux’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: For 21 and 31, ‘et’ is placed between the tens unit and the ones unit, so it reads as ‘20 and 1’ and ‘thirty and 1’ (e.g. ‘vingt et un’, ‘trente et un’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: In French, all nouns are either masculine or feminine, so they should be learnt with its corresponding gender and article.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The days of the week and the months are all masculine nouns.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: When writing, the days of the week and months of the year are not capitalised.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The names of most days in French come from the names of planets.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: French-speaking countries observe nationally significant religious and secular holidays (e.g. Christmas, Easter, and Bastille Day in France), alongside numerous seasonal cultural festivals (e.g. Carnaval de Québec).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Communicate about the days of the week, months, dates, and birthdays.
records.subject: French
records.section: Novice 1 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Because most French-speaking countries are in the Northern Hemisphere, their seasons are opposite to New Zealand’s; this reverses the timing of the school year and the nature of seasonal celebrations.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: In French, family members are often introduced using the phrase ‘Dans ma famille, il y a...’ (In my family, there is/are), followed by a list of relatives.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The subject pronouns ‘il’ and ‘elle’ are used for third person singular subjects, equivalent to ‘he’, ‘she’, and ‘it’ in English.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The conjunction ‘et’ is used to join multiples of 10 to the number 1 (e.g. ‘vingt et un’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: ‘Mon’ is the word for ‘my’ when the noun is masculine and singular, while ‘ma’ is used when the noun is feminine and singular.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Communicate about their families, including names and ages.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: In official and administrative contexts (such as on class rolls, school reports, and utility bills), the French generally follow the convention of writing a person’s surname first, in all capitals, and then given names. In everyday life, conversation, and personal correspondence, the Western standard of Given Name + Surname is routinely used.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Many languages use equivalent ‘tu’/’vous’ forms to indicate levels of respect or familiarity, such as German and Spanish. Other languages convey formality through different linguistic features (e.g. registers in Pacific languages).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Using the informal ‘tu’ when the formal ‘vous’ is required could come across as rude.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Masculine nouns take the indefinite article ‘un’, and feminine nouns take ‘une’. To talk about the quantity of an object, you replace ‘un’/’une’ by the number and use the plural form of the object.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Articles in French use grammatical gender and number (e.g. ‘un’/’une’, ‘le’/’la’, ‘des’, ‘les’) that agree with the noun.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: ‘Qu’est-ce que’ is a way of formulating a ‘what’ question.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: The phrase ‘il y a’ does not change between singular and plural — it means both ‘there is’ and ‘there are’.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Formulaic questions and answers may be used to express preference. These often include the verb ‘préférer’, ‘aimer’, and ‘détester’.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: The question word ‘quel’ or ‘quelle’ may be used to ask about preferences, and which one to use depends on the gender of the noun that follows.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Some words are spelt the same in English and French but are pronounced differently (e.g. orange).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Communicate in a classroom environment using an extended repertoire of instructions and short interactions.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Identify and communicate about classroom and school objects.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Express preferences, likes and dislikes in familiar contexts, and give reasons in a simple way where appropriate.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Cultural differences and regional traditions mean personal preferences — like food, school, sports, and music — often vary between New Zealand and French- speaking countries.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Many French words are used in English, particularly in the areas of food, fashion, and art (e.g. menu, chef, croissant, boutique, ballet, avant-garde).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: The form of the adjective must agree with the noun they qualify in gender (masculine or feminine). This change is reflected in both spelling and pronunciation.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: The conjugation of the verb ‘étre’ (to be) in the singular is: ‘je suis’, ‘tu es’, ‘il/elle/on est’.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: The conjugation of the verb ‘avoir’ (to have) in the singular is: ‘j’ai’, ‘tu as’, ‘il/elle a’.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Qualifiers (e.g. ‘très’, ‘assez’) can be used before the adjective to limit or intensify its meaning (e.g. ‘très timide’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Basic negation is formed with ‘ne … pas’, with the verb placed between the two words, such as in ‘Je ne suis pas drôle’, ‘ne’ is abbreviated to ‘n’’ before a vowel or silent ‘h’, such as in ‘Je n’ai pas…’.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Telling the time for both the 12-hour and 24-hour system uses ‘Il est [number] heure(s)’ when it is the exact hour. This base pattern may be immediately followed by 1–59 for the number of minutes past the hour (e.g. ‘Il est 16 heures vingt’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: When using the 12-hour system, terms such as ‘et quart’ and ‘et demie’ can be used to say quarter and half past the current hour (e.g. ‘Il est 4 heures et demie’), while ‘moins le quart’ and ‘moins [minutes]’ can be used to say quarter and the number of minutes to the next hour (e.g. ‘Il est 8 heures moins dix’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: The preposition ‘à’ is used to mean ‘at’ when talking about when an activity occurs.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Typically, the 24-hour clock is used to express time for specific contexts (e.g. schedules for transport and events). Otherwise, the 12-hour clock is used.
records.subject: French
records.section: Novice 2 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: In French, the vocabulary used to express ownership (such as ‘mon’, ‘ma’, or ‘mes’) must agree with the gender and number of the person or object being possessed.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: In French, the ‘s possessive structure does not exist. Expressing third person ownership is done through the [object] + ‘de’/’d’’ + [owner] pattern.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Questions can be formed simply by putting a question mark to the end of the sentence, without changing the word order.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: In most cases, plurals are formed by adding an ‘s’ to the end of a word, although the ‘s’ is not pronounced when speaking. Other words undergo significant changes in their plural form (e.g. the plural form of ‘un cheval’ is ‘des chevaux’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Some common French prepositions to indicate location are ‘sur’, ‘sous’, ‘devant’, and ‘derrière’.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Describe appearance and qualities of people, animals, and objects.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Tell the time.
records.subject: French
records.section: Novice 2 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Communicate about ownership.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Ask and answer simple questions about location.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: ‘Adorer’ can also be used to express a stronger like for som ething, while ‘détester’ can be used to express a stronger dislike. These verbs are followed by a noun or a verb in the infinitive form.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Words such as ‘beaucoup’ and ‘du tout’ are used to signify how strong a feeling is.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Different types of language resources and tools can be utilised for productive, receptive, and interactive skills (e.g. spellcheck, chatbots, online dictionaries).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Communication about activities and routines often includes adverbs of frequency (e.g. ‘souvent’), prepositions of location (e.g. ‘au parc’), and expressions of opinion (e.g. ‘j'aime’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Cognates are used for many school subjects (e.g. ‘la musique’, ‘les maths’, ‘l’histoire’) and sports (e.g. ‘le football’, ‘le basket’, ‘la danse’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: In French, two verbs are commonly used when discussing activities: ‘jouer’ for activities involving a ball, stick, or other equipment (e.g. ‘jouer à’ or o ‘je joue au foot’) and for musical instruments (e.g. ‘jouer de’ or ‘je joue de la guitare’) ‘faire de’ for most other sports and physical activities that don’t involve a ball or o equipment (e.g. ‘faire de la natation’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: When talking about certain routine activities such as waking, bathing, getting dressed, or going to bed, a reflexive verb is needed. These verbs use both a subject pronoun (e.g. ‘je’) and a matching reflexive pronoun (e.g. ‘me’) before the verb expressing an action which the subject does to themselves (e.g. ‘Je me lève’, ‘Il se couche’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: The prepositions ‘à’ and ‘de’ change form depending on the gender and number of the activity nouns they precede. For example: In front of a masculine singular noun, ‘à’ becomes ‘au’ and ‘de’ becomes ‘du’ o (e.g. ‘je joue au rugby’, ‘je fais du judo’) In front of a feminine singular noun, ‘à’ becomes ‘à la’ and ‘de’ becomes ‘de la’ o (e.g. ‘je joue à la pétanque’, ‘je fais de la natation’) In front of plural nouns, ‘à’ becomes ‘aux’ and ‘de’ becomes ‘des’ (e.g. ‘je joue o aux échecs’, ‘je fais des promenades’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: When ‘faire’ is used in the negative, it is followed by ‘de’ or ‘d’’ when the following noun starts with a vowel (e.g. ‘je ne fais pas de sports’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Verbs like ‘étudier’ and ‘jouer’ that finish in ‘er’ in the infinitive follow a regular conjugation pattern.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: The verbs ‘faire’ and ‘boire’ are irregular and are conjugated differently from regular –er verbs.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: The pronoun ‘on’ can mean ‘we’ when speaking casually, or it can mean ‘people’ or ‘one’. It takes the same verb form as ‘il’ and ‘elle’.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Words and phrases that express frequency can be positioned in several places within a sentence, except between the subject and the verb (e.g. ‘Je joue souvent’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: The pronunciation of the letter ‘g’ is either ‘soft’ (like the ‘s’ in measure) before ‘e’ or ‘i’, or ‘hard’ (like the ‘g’ in garden) before ‘a’, ‘o’, or ‘u’. To maintain the ‘soft’
records.subject: French

records.text: French speakers often avoid expressing feelings in extremes and instead prefer
records.subject: French

records.text: using measure expressions. Understating the preference for something is
records.subject: French

records.text: common and being too direct with dislikes can be seen as rude.

records.text: Expressing preferences is driven more by reason than emotion and sometimes
records.subject: French

records.text: involves discussing opinions on the topic.

records.text: Communicate about activities and routines, how often they are engaged in, and when and where they take place.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Express opinions about activities and give reasons where appropriate.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Daily life in Francophone countries follows a structured rhythm particularly around meals and school or work life, although the timing depends on the region and country (e.g. dinner may be between 7:30pm to 9pm in France but earlier in North American Francophone regions).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Extra-curricular activities are organised either through school or community clubs and associations.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Adverbs and prepositions of location identify and describe where people, places, or objects are situated (e.g. ‘sur la table, ‘devant l’école’, or ‘à côté du cinéma’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: French uses prepositions like ‘à’ and ‘de’ to form compound nouns (e.g. ‘salle de bains’, ‘salle à manger’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Possessive adjectives must agree in gender and number with the noun they modify, not with the owner.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: The phrase ‘il y a’ (there is) in the negative becomes ‘il n’y a pas de’ with no article needed afterwards.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: When talking about actions in the present, there is only one way to conjugate the verb. The distinction between simple present (e.g. ‘I go’) and present continuous (e.g. ‘I am going’) is understood from context. For example, ‘Elle va au musée’ could mean ‘She goes to a museum’ or ‘She is going to a museum.’
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: The character and architecture of towns and cities differ between countries and regions, reflecting their distinct histories and cultures.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: In France, living in an apartment is quite common, especially in urban areas.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Adjectives must agree in gender and number with the noun they qualify.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: In French, comparatives are expressed with ‘plus’ + [adjective] for ‘more than’ and ‘moins’ + [adjective] for ‘less than’. There is no way of adding a suffix to the adjective like –er in English.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: To communicate about future plans, the pattern [subject] + [conjugated verb for ‘go’ (aller)] + [infinitive of the main verb] is followed.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: To begin communicating about actions in the past, use regular –er verbs in the passé composé tense and formulaic use of ‘aller’ in 1st, 2nd, and 3rd person singular forms.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: For the regular –er verbs, the pattern [subject] + [present tense of the auxiliary verb ‘avoir’] + [past participle] is used. The past participle of regular –er verbs is formed by replacing the –er ending of the infinitive with ‘é’
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Communicate about a familiar place.

records.text: Formulaic expressions are paired with the verbs ‘vouloir’ (to want), ‘avoir besoin de’ (to need), ‘devoir’ (must/to owe), and ‘pouvoir’ (to be able to/can) to communicate desires, necessities, obligations, and permission.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Expressing wants can be done with the pattern: [subject] + [conjugated form of ‘vouloir’] + [infinitive form of main verb].
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Expressing needs or obligations can be done with several structures, such as: [subject] + [conjugated form of ‘avoir’] + ‘besoin de’ + [infinitive form of main o verb] [subject] + [conjugated form of ‘devoir’] + [infinitive form of main verb]. o
records.subject: French

records.text: Asking for and giving permission follows the same [subject] + [conjugated form of ‘pouvoir’] + [infinitive form of main verb] pattern, but asking for permission will end in a question mark.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The verbs ‘avoir’, ‘vouloir’, and ‘pouvoir’ are often used to ask for items or assistance in simple transactional contexts.
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The conditional form of ‘vouloir’ is used formulaically to make polite requests (e.g. ‘Je voudrais...’).
records.subject: French
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — French Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The preposition ‘de’ or ‘d’’ (for words beginning with a vowel) is used after expressions of quantity regardless of whether the noun which follows is masculine or feminine, singular or plural.
records.subject: French

records.text: Greetings in Japan show respect, hierarchy, and social connection.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: When greeting someone, bowing shows respect and maintains proper social distance.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Showing respect in Japanese culture can include: pronouncing words correctly o listening attentively o bowing appropriately. o
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: There are different greetings and forms of reference used in formal and informal situations. For example: こんにちは which can be used at any time o さようなら which can be used at school between teacher and student as a o farewell at the end of the day. It is rarely used in daily conversation because it implies a final, long-term farewell.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: When は is used in greetings, it is pronounced as ‘wa.’
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Use basic greetings and farewells in different contexts.
records.subject: Japanese
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: When asking for someone’s name, the polite prefix お is added to show respect.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Japanese uses particles to mark the grammatical role of words (e.g. topic, subject, object) in a sentence. They come directly after the word they are marking. Unlike English, which relies heavily on word order, Japanese relies on particles to create meaning.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Particles can have more than one function in a sentence.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The particle は can be used to mark the topic of a sentence and is pronounced ‘wa’ when used as a particle.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: です is the copula. It can be used to say what something or someone is (‘is ...’/‘am ...’/‘are ...’)
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: なん or なに is used to ask ‘What?’
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The sentence-ending particle か creates a question.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: [A] は [B] です（か) ([A] is [B]) is a basic Japanese sentence pattern.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Family plays an important role in Japanese culture, and families reuniting is a central theme in traditional festivals such as おしょうがつ (New Year) and おぼん (Obon).
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Family position is based on sibling age with older siblings addressed by their role and younger siblings by name.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Polite family terms are generally used by young people to talk to and about family members.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: います (the verb ‘to be’) is used to refer to animate things.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: います is used to express present positive and いません is used to express present negative.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: [Family term] + が + います is used to express who you have in your family.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The particle は can be used in a negative sentence.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The particle と can be used to join nouns in a complete list.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The particle の can be used to show possession.
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: Communicate about family members.

records.text: Japanese has two counting systems: Sino-Japanese numbers and native Japanese numbers.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Sino-Japanese numbers use numbers 1-10 as the foundation to count larger numbers.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Numbers are written by combining characters that show place value: o じゅういち (11) literally means 'ten-one' o にじゅう (20) literally means 'two-ten' にじゅういち (21) literally means ‘two-ten-one.’ o
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Four, seven, and nine each have two terms in Japanese, and which one is used depends on what is being counted.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: When counting different types of things, a classifier is added to the Sino-Japanese numbers.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: The classifier usually comes after the noun, and there is no particle between the classifier and the verb.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: The classifier for counting age is さい.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: ‘20 years old’ uses the native Japanese word はたち.
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: The particle も can be used to express ‘too,’ ‘also,’ ‘as well’ and goes directly after the word it relates to.
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: Festivals and seasonal activities in Japan often have historical and spiritual origins and carry cultural significance (e.g. Setsubun and Tanabata).
records.subject: Japanese
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: In Japan, each day of the week consists of a celestial body or natural element combined with the suffix ようび which means ‘day of the week.’
records.subject: Japanese
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Months are referred to in numerical order. For example: January is 1いちがつ o February is 2にがつ o April is しがつ o July is しちがつ o September is くがつ. o
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Communicate about the days of the week and months of the year.
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: [Noun] + particle が + すきです is used to express likes.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 12

records.text: The negative is [noun]+ particle は + すきじゃないです。
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 12

records.text: Adding だい (big) before すき or きらい intensifies the meaning of both words.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 12

records.text: すきじゃないです can be softer to use than きらいです depending on the context.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 12

records.text: あまり + negative (‘not much’) softens negative statements, making them more polite and less confrontational.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 12

records.text: The particle は can replace が in a negative sentence.
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: The particle や can be used to join nouns in an incomplete list.
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: Communication can be supported with set expressions for clarification, checking for understanding, asking for repetition, and asking for vocabulary translations.
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: Education and teachers are highly valued in Japan and there are set ways students should greet their teacher at the beginning of class. This is often combined with respectful gestures such as a student-initiated bow.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 12

records.text: Japanese has families of demonstrative words to point things out. These words begin with こ、そ、あ、ど
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: [Word] + particle は＋[language] + particle で＋なんですか is used to ask what a word means in another language.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 12

records.text: これ, それ, あれ mean ‘this’, ‘that (near you)’, and ‘that (over there)’ respectively.
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: Understand and respond to simple classroom language, politeness conventions, and formulaic expressions.

records.text: Japanese society places great importance on respectful address and honorifics.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: おじいさん and おばあさん can refer to elderly people in the community who are not relatives out of respect and friendliness.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Younger people call older people おじさん、おばさん、 おにいさん、 おねえさん, even though they are not part of the family.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Some greetings require cultural knowledge to be understood in translation, for example, understanding that おげんきですか is a genuine health enquiry rather than a greeting.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Suffixes are attached to names to show respect, social distance, or familiarity and the suffix used can change depending on the relationship. For example: ～さん is gender neutral and a polite way to address people o ～せんせい is used for teachers, doctors, and some other professionals o ～せんぱい is used for older students or more experienced colleagues in the o same group ～くん is used for young men, schoolboys, and among male peers o ～ちゃん is used for small children, babies, close friends (often females), and o pets.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Suffixes can be added to either the first or last name and are not used in reference to oneself.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Both せんせい and せんぱい can be used without a name as a direct title of address.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Use greetings and farewells in formal contexts.
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: [Country] + じん is used to express nationality.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: [Country] + からきました is used to express where one comes from, such as one’s roots or background.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: [School level] + ねんせい is used to express school grade at each level.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: [Place] に + すんでいます is used to express where one lives.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: Country names of foreign origin are generally written in katakana. Japan, China, and Korea are written in kanji.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: The family unit is important in Japan and all births, marriages, and deaths are recorded in an official household registry held by local and city offices where an entire family lineage is recorded on one continuous official document.
records.subject: Japanese
records.section: Novice 2 / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: Japanese nouns do not change form based on number (singular/plural), or definite/indefinite articles (a/an/the).
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: The classifier with Sino-Japanese numbers for three people upwards is にん (e.g. さんにん (three people), よにん (four people)).
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: ひとり (one person) and ふたり (two people) use the native Japanese system.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: Using です to count family members includes the speaker in the total number.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: [Pet] をかっています is used to express keeping a pet.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: The classifier for counting pets is ひき／びき／ぴき depending on the preceding number.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 14

records.text: Communicate about time.
records.subject: Japanese
records.section: Novice 2 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge /  Punctuality is highly valued in Japan, where it is seen as a sign of respect.  In writing, the 24-hour clock is often used, especially for formal, technical and public scheduling. /  The classifier for number of hours is じ and for minutes ふん.  [Number] じ + はん can be used when telling the time to express ‘half past’.  ごろ is used to express an approximate point of time.  In conversation, the time of day can be described as morning, day, or night (e.g. あ さの9じ, ひるの3じ, or よるの6じ).  ごぜん (am) or ごご (pm) goes before the time when precision is required without using 24-hour time. They are frequently used in business, schedules, and formal announcements.
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 15

records.text: Communicate about activities.
records.subject: Japanese
records.section: Novice 2 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Knowledge /  いきます and きます express movement relative to the speaker’s position at the time of speaking. /  The basic word order in Japanese is subject/topic–object–verb (SOV), where the main predicate comes at the end.  [Topic] は [noun] を [verb] is used to express someone/something does something, where the particle を is used to mark the direct object of an action.  [Topic] は [place] に [verb of motion] is used to express that someone is going, coming, and returning, where the particle に is used to mark the destination.  Verbs have a stem and an ending. The ending changes according to tense and polarity.  Japanese verbs have two tenses: past and non-past.  [Verb stem] ます is used to express what one does or is going to do.  [Verb stem] ません is used to express what one does not do habitually or is not going to do.  いつ is used to ask ‘When?’  The particle に can be used to mark a specific time.  A time word usually comes before or after the subject.  どこ is used to ask ‘Where?’  When answering どこ questions, the answer replaces どこ with the appropriate location word.  ここ(here)、そこ(there)、あそこ(over there) are demonstratives that refer to place.  The sentence-ending particle ねforms a tag question (e.g. ‘isn’t it?’).  The meaning of そうですか changes with the intonation. A falling tone means simple understanding (‘I see’), while a rising tone expresses surprise or a question (‘Is that so?’).
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 15

A falling tone means simple understanding (‘I see’), while a rising tone expresses surprise or a question (‘Is that so?’). /  Communicate about activities. / Asking and answering questions about places
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 15

records.text: There are two versions of the verb ‘to be’: あります for inanimate things, and いま す for animate things.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: There are two types of adjectives: い adjectives and な adjectives.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: Adjectives can be placed at the end of a sentence to act as the predicate.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: [Person] は [Body Part] が [adjective] です can be used to describe physical characteristics.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: [Noun] + particle が +じょうず です (good at/skilled in something) is usually used in reference to someone else.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: [Noun] + particle が + へた です (not good at, not skilled in something) can be used about oneself but rarely about others.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: この, その and あの are demonstratives used before a noun to mean ‘this’, ‘that (near you)’, and ‘that (over there)’, respectively.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: The sentence-ending particle よ adds assertion, telling the listener something new or with emphasis.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: Different types of language resources and tools can be utilised for productive, receptive, and interactive skills (e.g. spellcheck, chatbots, online dictionaries).
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: The order of information in Japanese usually starts with the more general then narrows down to more specific. For example, the family name first, then the given name. For addresses, the order is: postal code, prefecture, city, building. Dates follow the same pattern: year–month–date.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: The Western calendar is used in Japan in everyday contexts.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: Official documents sometimes use the Imperial Calendar which starts with the reign of the emperor.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: The 12 Japanese Zodiac animals are often used to discuss birth years and age and reflect on personality type.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: There are different words for the first ten days of a month, as well as the 20th, which are based on native Japanese readings.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: 14th and 24th are じゅうよっか and にじゅうよっか, respectively.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: The time suffixes 年（ねん）, 月（がつ）, and 日（にち） follow numbers for year, month, and day, respectively.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 18

records.text: Communicate about dates and birthdates.
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: Sentence connectives that go at the beginning of a sentence can: provide additional information (e.g. それに、そして、それから) o expand on something by giving reasons or consequences (e.g. それで、だから) o make a contrast (e.g. でも). o
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: The particles から and まで can be used to express ‘from’ and ‘until’/‘as far as’ for time and place.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 19

records.text: Being late in Japan is considered disrespectful because it causes inconvenience to others. Public transport arrives exactly on time and people arrive early when meeting someone.
records.subject: Japanese
records.section: Novice 3 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 19

records.text: Consistent prefixes can be used to indicate general time (e.g. せん (last...), こん (this…),らい (next...), and まい（every...).
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 19

records.text: Verb stem ました is used to express positive sentences in the past tense.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 19

records.text: Verb stem ませんでした is used to express negative sentences in the past tense.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 19

records.text: The particle に is not usually used after general time words.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 19

records.text: Japanese people often talk about the weather at the start of a conversation, using this to build rapport before moving into the main topic.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 19

records.text: There are four distinct seasons in Japan. The weather and seasons influence cultural activities such as はなみ in spring.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 19

records.text: どうですか can be used to ask how something is.

records.text: When adding time and place to a Japanese sentence, the usual order is topic/subject-time-place-object-verb (TTPOV).
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: The particle で can be used to mark the place where an action takes place.
records.subject: Japanese

records.text: Words of frequency can be placed at the beginning of a sentence or directly before the verb they modify.

records.text: The particle かcan be used between nouns to express ‘or’.

records.text: In Japanese culture, providing a reason relies on context, humility, and maintaining harmony.
records.subject: Japanese
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Japanese Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 20

records.text: どうして is a question word meaning ‘why’ and is used when asking the reason or cause for something.
