records.text: The verb endings used for classroom instructions change according to who is being addressed. For example: for one person (tú), the imperative ending (e.g. ‘habla’, ‘lee’) is used o for groups (vosotros), the final –r of the infinitive is replaced with –d (e.g. ‘hablad’, o ‘leed’) in more formal contexts (usted/ustedes), the present subjunctive form (e.g. o ‘hable’, ‘hablen’) is used.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Spanish uses different forms for giving commands; they are generally in the ‘you’ form, but with singular and plural options as well as regional variations between Spain and Latin America.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Communication can be supported with set expressions for clarification, checking for understanding, asking for repetition, and asking for vocabulary translations.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Formulaic questions and answers for identifying where a person is from, where they live, and what languages you speak often use the singular forms of the verbs ‘tener’, ‘vivir’, and ‘hablar’.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Respond to and use simple classroom language and politeness conventions.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 1 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Recognise the words for common classroom objects and expressions of location.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 1 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Exchange basic personal information.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Many Spanish-speaking countries have indigenous languages as well as other regional languages (e.g. Catalan and Basque in Spain).
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The numbers 16–19 in Spanish follow the same pattern where the ones unit is simply added onto the base ten, with a slight change in spelling and pronunciation (e.g. ‘diez’ + ‘seis’ becomes ‘dieciséis’, ‘diez’ + ‘nueve’ becomes ‘diecinueve’).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: In Spanish, all nouns are either masculine or feminine. Generally, nouns ending in –o are masculine and nouns ending in –a are feminine. However, there are exceptions to this rule, so it is recommended to learn the article in conjunction with the noun.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The masculine plural is used for mixed-gender groups.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The days of the week and the months are all masculine nouns.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: In Spanish, the days of the week and the months are not capitalised.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The names of the days of the week in Spanish reflect historical and religious influences from different traditions, including Roman mythology, Christianity, and earlier celestial naming traditions linked to the moon and planets.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Spanish-speaking countries observe religious holidays like Christmas and Easter, alongside nationally significant secular holidays (e.g. Mexico’s Independence Day) and seasonal traditions (e.g. Las Fallas in Spain).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Birthday celebrations in Spanish-speaking countries share some traditions but also vary across countries and regions.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: In Spanish, the verb ‘hacer’ is used to describe general weather conditions (e.g. ‘hace sol’ for ‘it is sunny’), while verbs such as ‘llover’ and ‘nevar’ are used to describe specific weather events.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Impersonal verbs conjugated in the third person singular are used to talk about the weather.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Spanish-speaking countries span both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, so seasonal changes occur at different times of the year.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The possessive adjectives ‘mi’, ‘tu’, and ‘su’ do not change for gender but do agree in number with the noun (e.g. ‘mi abuelo’, ‘mis abuelos’, ‘tu gato’, ‘tus gatos’).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Most plurals are formed by adding –s to nouns ending in a vowel and –es to nouns ending in a consonant.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The negative ‘no’ goes before the verb (e.g. ‘No tengo hermanos’).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: While ‘padre’ in the singular means ‘father’, the plural form ‘padres’ means both ‘parents’ and ‘fathers’ and therefore refers to both mother and father.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Communicate about the days of the week, months, dates, and birthdays.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 1 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Communicate about the weather and the seasons.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 1 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Communicate about families, including names and ages.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Extended family may live in the same household.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: In Spanish-speaking cultures, people typically use two family names, keeping their paternal and maternal surnames.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Many languages (e.g. French and German) use equivalent ‘tú’/‘usted’ forms to indicate levels of respect or familiarity. Other languages convey formality through different linguistic features (e.g. registers in Pacific languages).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Using the informal ‘tú’ when the formal ‘usted’ is required could be perceived as rude.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: The verb ‘hay’ means both ‘there is’ and ‘there are’ — it does not change between singular and plural.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Articles in Spanish use grammatical gender and number (un/una, el/la, unos/unas, los/las) that agree with the noun.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Adjectives like ‘bueno’ (good), ‘malo’ (bad), ‘interesante’ (interesting), and ‘aburrido’ (boring) are used to provide basic reasons for preferences.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: The verb ‘gustar’ (to please) is used to talk about likes or dislikes.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: The pronoun before ‘gusta(n)’ (me, te, le, nos, les) reflects the person doing the liking or disliking (literally who is being pleased or not pleased).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: The construction ‘gusta(n)’ + [definite article] + [noun] is used to express liking a thing (e.g. ‘Me gusta el español’).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: ‘Gustar’ is conjugated to agree with the thing being discussed. For example, ‘I like mathematics’ is ‘Me gustan las matemáticas’ (literally meaning ‘Mathematics pleases me’), with ‘gustan’ conjugated to agree with ‘las matemáticas’.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: The singular form ‘gusta’ is used with infinitive verbs (–ar, –er, –ir) to express liking an action.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Dislike is expressed by placing ‘no’ before ‘me gusta(n)’.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Communicate in a classroom environment using an extended repertoire of instructions and short interactions.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Identify and communicate about classroom and school objects.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Express preferences and likes and dislikes in familiar contexts and give reasons in a simple way where appropriate.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 11

records.text: Preferences in areas such as food, school subjects, after-school activities, sports, and music may vary between New Zealand and Spanish-speaking countries due to cultural influences and regional traditions.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: In Spanish, adjectives must agree with the noun they qualify in both gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: This also applies to possessive adjectives: mi(s), tu(s), su(s), nuestro/a(s), vuestro/a(s).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Adjectives generally follow the nouns they describe, a structure that is similar to te reo Māori but different from English.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: The negative ‘no’ goes before the verb meaning ‘to be’ (e.g. ‘No soy alta’).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: A variety of question words are needed to find out about people (e.g. ‘¿Cómo?’, ‘¿Qué?’, ‘¿Dónde?’, ‘¿Cuál?’).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: What is considered polite or appropriate when describing someone’s appearance may vary across cultures and contexts. Spanish often uses physical descriptors as neutral identifiers (e.g. ‘la morena’, ‘el rubio’).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: The verb ‘ser’ is used to tell the time, and it changes from ‘es’ to ‘son’ to agree with the time in number (e.g. ‘es la una’, ‘son las dos’).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Most Spanish-speaking countries use the 12-hour clock, while some, like Argentina, use the 24-hour clock.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Perceptions of punctuality are varied across Spanish-speaking cultures. While business and formal appointments are often treated with timeliness, social gatherings are more flexible.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: You can form a question in Spanish simply by adding an inverted question mark (¿) at the beginning of a declarative sentence and a standard question mark (?) at the end, without changing the order of the words.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Most plurals in Spanish are formed by adding –s to words ending in a vowel and –es to words ending in a consonant.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Words used for everyday objects may vary across Spanish-speaking countries (e.g. ‘ordenador’/‘computadora’). These differences may cause confusion but generally will not lead to major breakdown in communication as similar grammar and sentence structures make it easy to imply meaning from context.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 2 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociocultural / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: As in te reo Māori, adjectives follow nouns and agree in gender and number with the noun they follow.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Some common Spanish prepositions are ‘en’, ‘al lado de’, and ‘entre’.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: The preposition ‘de’ and the definite article ‘el’ contract to become ‘del’.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Spanish has two words for ‘to be’, namely: ‘ser’, used for permanent or lasting qualities (e.g. identity, characteristics, origin), o and to talk about time, days, dates, and seasons ‘estar’, used for temporary states or conditions (e.g. location, feelings, temporary o conditions, actions in progress).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Describe appearance and qualities of people, animals, and objects.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 2 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Tell the time.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 2 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Communicate about ownership.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 2 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociocultural / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Ask and answer simple questions about location.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Levels of directness when expressing opinions may vary across Spanish-speaking communities and contexts. Being direct does not mean they are being rude.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: In Spanish, verbs in the infinitive end in –ar, –er, or –ir. They follow regular patterns by changing their endings to reflect person, number, and tense.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: The Spanish words for many school subjects (e.g. ‘historia’, ‘física’, ‘música’) and sports (e.g. ‘fútbol’, ‘tenis’, ‘voleibol’) are cognates of their English equivalents.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: For ball sports and games, the verb ‘jugar’ is used followed by ‘a’ and the definite article. ‘Jugar’ follows an irregular verb conjugation pattern.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: For non-ball sports, the verb ‘practicar’ or ‘hacer’ is used, immediately followed by the sport.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Other verbs to use with activities include ‘tener’, ‘estudiar’, ‘mirar’, ‘leer’, and ‘escuchar’.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Words and phrases that express frequency can be positioned in several places in the sentence, like in English.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: While in English people say ‘on Mondays’, in Spanish people say ‘los lunes’ (literally ‘the Mondays’).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Spanish uses reflexive forms of verbs and pronouns to indicate certain daily routines.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: School timetables, extracurricular activities, and daily routines may differ across cultures and contexts, though may tend to follow a structured rhythm (e.g. dinner times in some countries are much later than others; some Spanish-speaking countries have a ‘siesta’, or a midday rest where people sleep or businesses close).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Communicate about activities and routines, how often one engages in them, and when and where they take place.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 3 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Express opinions about activities and give reasons where appropriate.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 3 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 13

records.text: Prepositions of location are used with ‘estar’ to describe where people, places, and objects are located.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: The verbs ‘seguir’, ‘girar’, ‘tomar’, and ‘haber’ are used to give directions to get from one place to the other.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: The verb ‘estar’ is used to indicate where a place is located.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Directions are provided using imperative forms that change based on the recipient (singular or plural).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Where English uses just two nouns to form a compound noun (e.g. science classroom), Spanish uses the preposition ‘de’ between the nouns (e.g. ‘aula de ciencias’).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: In Spanish, comparatives are expressed with ‘más [adjective] que’ for ‘more than’ and ‘menos [adjective] que’ for ‘less than’. One does not simply add a suffix to the adjective, as is done with adding –er in English.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Adverbs of degree (e.g. ‘un poco’, ‘muy’) go before the adjective.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: ‘Ir’ is an irregular high-frequency verb.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: The sentence structure for the immediate future follows the pattern ‘[conjugated form of ‘ir’] + a + [infinitive of the main verb]’, with ‘ir’ conjugated as ‘voy’, ‘vas’, ‘va’, ‘vamos’, ‘vais’, or ‘van’.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Uncertain conditions can be referred to using ‘si + [present tense clause]’ in combination with another clause.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: To begin communicating about actions in the past, regular verbs are used in either the Pretérito Perfecto (European Spanish) or Pretérito Indefinido (Latin American Spanish) tenses, as well as formulaic use of the verbs ‘ir’ and ‘hacer’ in the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd person singular forms.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: For regular verbs in the Pretérito Perfecto, the present tense form of ‘haber + [past participle of main verb]’ is used. The past participles are formed by: replacing the infinitive ending of regular –ar verbs with –ado o replacing the infinitive ending of regular –er and –ir verbs with –ido. o
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Regular verbs in the Pretérito Indefinido are formed by removing the –ar/–er/–ir ending from the infinitive and adding the correct verb ending based on the subject. For example: For –ar verbs, add –é (I), –aste (you), and –ó (he/she) o For –er and –ir verbs, add –í (I), –iste (you), and –ió (he/she). o
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: The tenses used when talking about the past differ based on region. European Spanish speakers tend to prefer using the Pretérito Perfecto tense, while Latin American Spanish speakers tend to prefer the Pretérito Indefinido tense.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Communicate about a familiar place.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Ask for and give directions.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Make simple comparisons between people, places, or things.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Communicate about a limited range of actions in the past, and plans for the immediate future.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 3 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Use time markers referring to the past and immediate future to add more detail.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 3 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: The imperative can be used to make a request.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The direct object pronoun has different forms depending on the person(s) or object(s) it refers to.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The direct object pronoun goes before the conjugated verb or is attached at the end of the imperative.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Spanish transactional requests do not necessarily use the same markers of courtesy as English (e.g. use of imperatives to place an order in a bar or restaurant would not be considered rude).
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Negotiating the price of an item is culturally acceptable in certain contexts and locations.
records.subject: Spanish
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Use simple language to interact in transactional contexts.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 3 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Communicate about quantity and cost of items.
records.subject: Spanish
records.section: Novice 3 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Spanish Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Different greetings and farewells are used depending on context and the number of people being addressed.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: ‘Kia ora’ is commonly used to say hello, express thanks, and show agreement. The literal meaning of the phrase expresses the hope of wellness for someone.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: There are unique dialects evident across iwi and regions with differences in pronunciation and vocabulary. Not every speaker of te reo Māori who has whakapapa to a particular iwi or lives in a region will observe dialectical differences. Some examples of dialectal differences are: Ngāi Tahu – k’ replaces ‘ng’ o Tūhoe – ‘ng’ becomes ‘n’ o Taranaki – ‘h’ is often dropped (e.g. Whanganui is pronounced ‘Wanganui’) o Ngāpuhi – ‘w’ is often dropped (e.g. ‘whakarongo’ is pronounced ‘hakarongo’). o
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Hongi and harirū are gestures that are often a part of formal and informal greetings, where: hongi involves the pressing of noses and symbolises the sharing of hā (the o breath) harirū is a handshake and is a loan word formed from the phrase ‘how do you o do’. Harirū can be used alongside or instead of hongi in both formal and informal settings.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: The greeting ‘ata mārie’ is a modern phrase created as a translation of the English phrase ‘good morning’. Other ways to greet someone in the morning would be ‘ngā mihi o te ata’ or ‘mōrena’.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: The farewell ‘pō mārie’ is a modern phrase created as a translation of the English phrase ‘good night’; it cannot be used as a greeting in the evening. A way to farewell someone in the evening would be ‘ngā mihi o te pō’.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Although referring to someone using a term of address (e.g. boy, elderly woman) may be considered rude in other cultures, this is not the case in te reo Māori.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Referring to someone as your friend in te reo may not necessarily mean that they are a friend; it is a widely used term in te ao Māori.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Waiata are an integral part of te ao Māori and can be used to enhance mihi (greetings or introductions) in a variety of contexts.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Te arapū Māori (the Māori alphabet) contains vowels, consonants, digraphs, and macrons.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Te reo Māori has five vowels (a, e, i, o, u), each with a short and long form.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Every Māori word ends in a vowel.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: A tohutō (macron) marks a long vowel sound and can change the meaning of a word (e.g. wahine means woman, and wāhine meaning women, ‘kēkē’ means armpit, ‘keke’ means cake).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Some syllable sounds in te reo Māori can be challenging for learners and may require extra practise. These include syllables that begin with ng, r, t, and wh. The digraph ‘ng’ is pronounced as it is in the words ‘singer’, ‘bringing’, and o ‘Singapore’. The letter ‘r’ in te reo Māori is tapped, not rolled. The tongue taps the roof of the o mouth to produce the sound. The letter ‘t’ is pronounced two different ways – this is determined by the vowel o that follows it. When paired with ‘a’, ‘e’, and ‘o’, the ‘t’ is said softly, and when paired with ‘i’ and ‘u’, it is aspirated. The digraph ‘wh’ is usually pronounced like an English ‘f’. o
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: ‘Ka kite’ does not literally mean ‘see you’ – it is a shortened version of a longer phrase ‘ka kite au i a koe’ and is widely accepted as a colloquial farewell. Second person pronouns can’t be added directly after the phrase when used as a farewell due to the structure of the longer grammatically correct phrase.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Use greetings and farewells appropriately for a range of different contexts.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Apply knowledge of pronunciation.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 8

records.text: Introductions and greetings are a way to establish whanaungatanga and link to broader core values such as whānau, aroha, and manaakitanga.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: In te ao Māori, introducing your whānau is important because it helps people understand who you are and where you come from, and builds respectful connections.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Pronouns are not gendered, meaning the pronoun ‘ia’ can mean he, she, or they (one person).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: In English, it is usually considered rude to ask someone ‘Who are you?’ as it may imply challenge rather than genuine interest. In te ao Māori, it is not considered rude to ask someone ‘Ko wai koe?’
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Asking how someone is can be shortened to phrases such as ‘Kei te pēhea?’ or ‘E pēhea ana?’. In some hapū/iwi, the phrase ‘Kei te aha?’ is used to ask how someone is feeling.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: There are singular, dual, and plural pronouns and different words for "we" and "us" that allow speakers to clearly identify exactly who is being referred to.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: ‘Ko’ can be used before a personal name when introducing oneself or someone else.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The pronouns ‘au’ and ‘ahau’ both mean I/me.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Replying to the question ‘Ko wai tō ingoa?’ requires some simple word replacements: the interrogative word ‘wai’ (who) is replaced with the name of the person o the relational particle ‘tō’ (your) becomes ‘taku’ (my). o
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Communicating about whānau members can use the same sentence pattern as how to say your name.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The words ‘rāua ko’ is used to link two people’s names when talking about them.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The letter ‘t’ is removed from most singular relational particles to make them plural (e.g. ‘taku hoa’ is used for my friend, while ‘aku hoa’ is used for my friends).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Relational particles are connected to personal pronouns (e.g. ‘taku’ goes with ‘au’/’ahau’ (I), ‘tō’ goes with ‘koe’ (you), ‘tōna’ goes with ‘ia’ (he/she/they)). Understanding these connections enables accurate use of relational particles when describing people and their relationship with something or someone else.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The phrase to ask how people are is made up of the verbal particles ‘kei te’ or ‘e ___ ana’, the word ‘pēhea’ which means ‘how’, and the relevant pronoun.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: In response to questions about how one is feeling, the word ‘pēhea’ is replaced with a relevant answer.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: When communicating about the number of people, both the ‘e hia’ and the ‘tokohia’ structures can be used. The ‘tokohia’ structure can only be used when counting people.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: There are similarities between words in te reo Māori and other Polynesian languages as they share origins. For example: ‘rua’ – te reo Māori o Aotearoa and te reo Māori Kūki ‘Airani o ‘lua’ – gagana Sāmoa o ‘ua’ – lea Faka-Tonga/vagahau Niue o ‘‘elua’ – ‘ōlelo Hawai`i. o
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Cardinal numbers follow a consistent structure made up of number bases, place value, and patterns.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Base numbers (1–10) are used to build larger numbers using patterns and place value knowledge.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: In response to questions about number, ‘E hia’ is replaced with a relevant answer.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: When counting in te reo Māori: the word ‘kotahi’ paired with the determiner ‘te’ (or similar marker) is used for o one item the particle ‘e’ comes before the numbers 2-9 and is not required when a o number starts with a 1 (e.g. 1, 10, 100). ‘E’ is also never used after the word mā.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: The determiner ‘ngā’ (or similar plural marker) is used for plural objects.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Introduce self and others and respond to introductions appropriately.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: Ask how others are and respond appropriately.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 1 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 9

records.text: In te ao Māori, introducing yourself may include talking about your connections to people, places, and whakapapa.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The concept of home is subjective and may reflect where a person feels they belong, not necessarily where they reside.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: ‘Kei’ is used to indicate present location, such as current place of residence.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The particle ‘ko’ can be used before place names to indicate where one’s home is.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: In response to questions, the interrogative words (e.g. ‘hea’, ‘wai’) are often replaced with the relevant answer.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The use of the word 'te' after the word 'ko' before a day of the week or a month is optional.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Definite articles differ depending on whether something is singular or plural: ‘te’ can be used for one item (singular), such as ‘te whare’, and ‘ngā’ can be o used for more than one item (plural), such as ‘ngā whare’ ‘he’ can be used for plural or singular, such as ‘He pene tēnei’/’He pene ēnei’ o ‘kei’ is used to say where something currently is and connects to locative o indicators, such as ‘konei’ (here) and ‘konā’ (there, by you) ‘tēnei’, ‘tēnā’, and ‘tērā’ (and their plural forms ‘ēnei’, ‘ēnā’, and ‘ērā’) are used o to show where things are in relation to the speaker and the listener.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The particle ‘i’ is written as a lowercase letter in the middle of a sentence, unlike in English, where ‘I’ is always capitalised as a pronoun.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: When talking about actions we state the verbal particle/s, then the verb, and then the performer of the action.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The verbal particles ‘kei te’ can indicate the present tense.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: The question word ‘aha’ means ‘what’ and is used when inquiring about actions.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Communicate about where things are located.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Communicate about activities in the present.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 10

records.text: Using simple classroom language in te reo Māori supports the consistent use and fosters confidence and familiarity over time.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: In nominal sentences, the adjective often follows the noun to describe the object.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: There are different karakia for different purposes, such as beginning and ending a gathering, supporting learning, offering protection, promoting well-being, or acknowledging environment.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Karakia can be heard at marae, schools, and in other social settings.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Karakia predate the arrival of Christianity to New Zealand.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Many karakia are meditative rather than religious.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Religious prayers can be referred to as inoi to differentiate them from karakia and should only be utilised in appropriate settings.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Learning and reciting simple karakia supports confidence and helps to develop vocabulary and correct pronunciation.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Learning karakia takes time and requires regular practice so that the words and meanings become familiar and understood.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: It is important that karakia (or inoi) are appropriate to the context.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Understand and use simple classroom language.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: Participate respectfully in karakia for different purposes.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 1, page 11

records.text: The way to address someone reflects the relationship with the person and the context.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 2 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Interactions should be guided by whanaungatanga, manaakitanga, and tikanga.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 2 / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: When addressing people using their names, ‘e’ precedes names when the name is a Māori name with fewer than three vowels.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: When addressing people using a term of address, ‘e’ precedes terms of address with fewer than three vowels.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: When addressing people using a term of address, the word ‘mā’ follows terms of address to make them plural.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: In direct address, titles and collective nouns are proceeded by words such as ‘e te’ or ‘e ngā’.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Short vowels are often incorrectly lengthened despite not being marked with macrons (e.g. kia, ata, mihi); long vowels are often incorrectly shortened despite being marked with macrons (e.g. āpōpō, mōrena, tēnā).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: The tuakana-teina relationship is a traditional way of understanding roles and responsibilities between older and younger siblings or relatives and is deeply connected to whakapapa.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Some words to express siblings are unique as they refer to gender and age: ‘tuakana’ – older sibling of the same gender o ‘teina’ – younger sibling of the same gender o ‘tungāne’ – brother of a female o ‘tuahine’ – sister of a male. o
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Kaumātua (elders) and whānau whānui (extended family) can have important roles in guiding, supporting, and maintaining the well-being of the whānau.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Kaumātua can share wisdom and uphold tikanga, while whānau whānui work together to nurture identity, belonging, and collective responsibility.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: The words ‘rātou ko’ are used to link three or more people’s names when talking about who someone is related to.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: A ‘tohutō’ is also added to pluralise some nouns that reference people (e.g. ‘teina’ (single) becomes ‘tēina’ (plural)).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Some words have a macron whether they are plural or not (e.g. ‘tāne’, ‘tungāne’).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: ‘Tokohia’ is used when asking about the number of people, never objects or other things.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: The prefix ‘toko’ is used before numbers 2-9.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: There is no neutral category of the word ‘of’ – it is only ‘a’ or ‘o’.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: The word ‘a’ to mean ‘of’ is used for relationships where one typically looks after the person, such as in generations below the person and in spousal relationships (e.g. ‘tamāhine’, ‘tama’, ‘tamariki’, ‘mokopuna’, ‘irāmutu’, ‘tāne’, ‘whaiāipo’).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: The word ‘o’ to mean ‘of’ is used for relationships where one is typically looked after by the person, such as in the same generation or in the generations above the person (e.g. ‘tuakana’, ‘teina’, ‘tungāne’, kaihana’, ‘māmā’, ‘whaea kēkē’, ‘mātua’, ‘tipuna’).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Use names and terms of address with greetings and farewells.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 2 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Knowledge / Linguistic
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Apply knowledge of pronunciation.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 2 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Cultural and Sociolinguistic / Knowledge / Linguistic
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Communicate about whānau relationships.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 2 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 12

records.text: Sentences beginning with ‘he’ can be used to describe physical characteristics and personality traits.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Intensifiers/adverbs (e.g. ‘tino’, ‘rawa’) can be added to emphasise the adjective in a sentence.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: The phrase 'rā whānau' references birth date (e.g. the day someone was born) as opposed to 'huritau' which means birthday.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Ordinal numbers are formed by adding the prefix ‘tua’ to base numbers 1-9 (e.g. ‘tuatahi’, ‘tuarua’, ‘tuaiwa’).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: In dates, numbers are written as numerals.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: After ‘tuaiwa’, the prefix ‘tua’ is no longer required (e.g. ‘tekau’, ‘tekau mā tahi’).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: The use of the word ‘te’ before a day of the week is optional.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: People can have connections to multiple hapū, iwi, and whenua through different members of their whānau.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: ‘Nō’ refers to whakapapa or genealogical connections to a place and is a useful structure to use when describing ethnic or cultural background. This structure can be used to reference iwi and hapū, as well as places.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: The question word ‘hea’ means ‘where’ and is used when inquiring about place.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: The particle ‘a’ is used before a person’s name when talking about them.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Standardised time expressions follow analogue clock conventions.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: 'He aha te wā?' translates to 'What is time?' as opposed to 'What is the time?'.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: The particle ‘i’ indicates minutes past the hour.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: The particle ‘ki’ indicates minutes to the hour.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: There are two common words used for the word time, namely ‘wā’ and the loan word ‘tāima’.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: The words ‘i te’ can be used to mark the time of the day (e.g. i te ahiahi).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Communication can be supported with set expressions for clarification, checking for understanding, asking for repetition, and asking for vocabulary translations.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Use simple descriptive language to describe people and things.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Communicate about dates and birthdates.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Communicate about place of origin and relationships between people.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 2 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Knowledge / Linguistic
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Communicate about time.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: Understanding and using a wider variety of classroom language and formulaic expressions.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 2, page 13

records.text: A mihi is a greeting, acknowledgement, or introduction that includes acknowledging places, people, and space in both formal and informal contexts.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Mihi are a way of upholding the values of manaakitanga and whanaungatanga.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Mihimihi is the process of multiple people sharing mihi to create connections.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Mihimihi is a time when non-Māori can share their ancestral connections to where they come from, while acknowledging and paying tribute to the whenua they now stand upon in New Zealand.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Māori may choose to include pepeha elements in mihi as a way of introducing oneself through sharing whakapapa, connections to whenua, ancestral waka, and significant landmarks such as mountains and rivers.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: The words ‘te/taku’ and ‘ngā/aku’ are often used interchangeably when referencing pepeha elements such as maunga. These words do not denote possession but instead indicate relationship.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: From a Māori worldview, pepeha are a treasure handed down by tīpuna (ancestors).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: As an alternative to pepeha, non-Māori can include kōrero tuakiri (statements of identity).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: There are dialectical differences that may impact structure, words, or sounds in mihi: ahau/au/awau o tīpuna/tūpuna o kāinga/kāika. o
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Whakataukī are proverbs of which the origin is unknown; whakatauākī are sayings in which the original speaker/author is known.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Whakataukī and whakatauākī can be used to express cultural values, place, whakapapa, knowledge, historical events, and learnings.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Relational particles are categorised into ‘a’ and ‘o’ relationships. For example, ‘tāku’ and ‘tōku’ both mean ‘my’. The word used is determined by the relationship between the relational particle and the noun that follows it.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: To determine which word is used, the nature of the relationship between the two things must be determined. For example, ‘my horse’ would be ‘tāku hōiho’ if the horse is being referenced as a pet that one cares for (nurturance = ‘a’ relationship). In contrast, ‘tōku hōiho’ is used if the horse is being referenced as a means of transport (transport = 'o’ relationship).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: There are no tribal variations to ‘a’ and ‘o’ relationships. Tuhinga, waiata, and other kōrero tuku iho show this.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: There are different forms of relational particles based on whether the relational particle is singular or plural. For example: ‘o’ relationship: ‘tōku kuia’ (my grandmother) ‘ōku kuia’ (my grandmothers), o ‘a’ relationship: ‘taku tamāhine’ (my daughter), ‘aku tamāhine’ (my daughters). o
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Communicate about connection to place in formal contexts.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: Communicate about relationships using relational particles.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 3 / Cultural and sociolinguistic knowledge / Linguistic / knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 14

records.text: The verbal particles ‘e ___ ana’ and ‘kei te’ can both be used to speak about an action in the present tense. The verb sits between the verbal particles ‘e’ and ‘ana’.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The verbal particle ‘i’ denotes the simple past tense, indicating that an action occurred in the past.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The verbal particle ‘ka’ can be used to communicate in the future tense.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: ‘Ka’ is pronounced as a long vowel sound when it is followed by a word with two vowels (e.g. ka kite).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The question word ‘aha’ means ‘what’ and is used when inquiring about actions.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Loan words are used for modern forms of transportation (e.g. ‘pahi’, ‘tereina’, ‘paihikara’).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: While the word ‘waka’ is the word for traditional voyaging vessels, it is used widely in reference to cars and vehicles in general.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The particle ‘mā’ indicates the method or means of travel, in the phrase ‘mā runga’, it is followed by a type of vehicle to specify the mode of transport being used.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The phrase ‘mā raro’ is a fixed expression meaning travelling ‘by foot’.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The word 'hea' means where and is used to enquire about location.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: When referencing location, the particle 'ki' means 'to'.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Communicating likes and dislikes within a Māori context involves understanding and respecting the perspectives of others, acknowledging collective values, and upholding tikanga. This is essential for nurturing whanaungatanga.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: While monetary value can be directly stated, Māori culture often places greater emphasis on reciprocity, meaning that what has been given should be met with equal respect or contribution.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Koha is the concept of giving from the heart without fixed value where cost is relative to relationship and context.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Adjectives are used to describe the quality or characteristics of things, such as ‘maoa’ (cooked), ‘reka’ (sweet/delicious), and ‘pirau’ (rotten).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The maramataka is a traditional Māori calendar that tracks the moon, sun, and stars. Seasonal changes guide activities like planting, fishing, and harvesting.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Weather and seasons are connected to maramataka.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The phrase ‘he pai ki’ can be used to communicate about likes. When using a

records.text: The word ‘me’ is used to join common nouns.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: ‘Kāore’ is used to show negation when something isn’t liked.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: ‘Nā te mea’ is used to justify and helps connect ideas.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Communicate about past, present, and future events and experiences.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Communicate about travel to and from locations.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 3 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Knowledge / Linguistic
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Communicate about likes and dislikes and justify where appropriate.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 3 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Knowledge / Linguistic
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Communicate about quality, quantity, and cost.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 3 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Knowledge / Linguistic
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: Communicate about the weather and seasons.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 15

records.text: The question word ‘pēhea’ means ‘how’ and is used when inquiring about current weather conditions.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Describing weather usually requires a verb (e.g. ‘the rain is falling’ not ‘it is raining’).
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: ‘Ko’ is a particle that is used when talking about something specific, such as the current season.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: In te reo Māori, politeness is expressed through manner, delivery, and tone.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: There is no direct translation for the word ‘please’ in te reo Māori.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: The word ‘e’ is added before verbs with one long vowel or two short vowels to form a command. For commands with more than two short vowels, the ‘e’ is omitted.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: The word ‘me’ is added before verbs to indicate that something should happen.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: The directional particles ‘mai’, ‘atu’, ‘iho’ and ‘ake’ can be added after verbs to add direction to commands.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: The word ‘homai’ is used when requesting for someone to give you something.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: ‘Kaua e ___’ is used to instruct someone not to do an action.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: ‘Kāti te ___’ is used to instruct someone to stop doing an action.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: In traditional Māori culture, narratives were primarily communicated orally and are passed down through generations to preserve knowledge, values, and identity.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Knowledge from the past is shared through oral forms such as whaikōrero, mōteatea, waiata, karanga, haka, and pūrākau.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Complex narratives, whakapapa, and mātauranga ā-iwi/ ā-hapū can be conveyed through visual story art forms such as whakairo, raranga, and tukutuku.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: The verbal particle ‘i te’ denotes the past continuous tense and indicates that an action was occurring in the past.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: The verbal particle ‘kua’ can be used to describe past, present, and future tense; when used in the past tense, it is similar to the English words ‘have’ and ‘has’.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Time adverbs can be used to add more specificity about when an action occurred.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Kīwaha are colloquial expressions or phases that reflect cultural values, humour, emotion, and social norms. They add richness and authenticity to everyday conversations.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Kīwaha add nuance and depth to communication, strengthening social bonds and conveying meaning efficiently.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: The meaning of kīwaha is most often figurative, not literal.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Give and follow basic instructions.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 3 / Linguistic Knowledge / Cultural and / Sociolinguistic / Knowledge / Linguistic
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: Use simple narratives in the past tense.
records.subject: Te Reo Māori
records.section: Novice 3 / Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge / Linguistic Knowledge
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Te Reo Māori Years 0–10, September 2026, Novice 3, page 16

records.text: The Silk Roads, developed during China’s Han Dynasty (202 BCE–220 CE), were a vast network of trade routes linking the east (China) to the west (Europe). records.text: In response, European nations along the Atlantic seaboard, such as Spain and Portugal, followed later by England, France, and the Netherlands, sought new sea routes to East Asia, leading to what has become known as the Age of Exploration (roughly 15th to 17th centuries). records.text: This led to Hōne Heke's (Ngāpuhi) flagstaff protests and the Northern War (1845–1846), the first major conflict between the Crown and a Māori force led by Hōne Heke Pōkai and Te Ruki Kawiti (Ngāpuhi). While they were supported by some Ngāpuhi and allied Māori, other influential Ngāpuhi leaders, especially Tāmati Wāka Nene, sided with the Crown.

records.text: Ruapekapeka Pā is the site of the defining battle of the war and remains an important historical and cultural site.

records.text: Māori worked to protect their people’s whenua (land), language, culture, and authority. For example, Māori leaders such as Sir Āpirana Ngata (Ngāti Porou) and Sir Māui Pōmare (Ngāti Mutunga, Ngāti Toa) worked within political and government systems to improve Māori social, economic, and cultural well- being while maintaining Māori identity and aspirations.

records.text: The loss of Māori land led to responses, including the Kiingitanga movement, Parihaka resistance, the 1975 Land March, and Treaty settlement processes.

records.text: Concerns about the loss of te reo Māori led to Māori advocacy groups campaigning for language revitalisation, for example, Ngā Tamatoa and the 1972 Māori Language Petition, kōhanga reo, and kura kaupapa Māori.

records.text: Starting with the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, many people such as farmers and miners in North America, motivated by the belief in Manifest Destiny, moved west for new land, jobs, and better lives.

records.text: Ranching and cowboys driving huge herds of cattle were two major economic activities. The 1849 California Gold Rush increased the population and development of the area, with both positive and negative effects.
