records.section: Global history / Expansion west in America (1803–1890s)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 33

records.text: Settlers and Native American peoples came into conflict as both sought control of land and resources, and westward expansion reshaped the lives of everyone involved. Ongoing conflict with Native American peoples, including the Sioux Wars, led to tragic events such as the Wounded Knee Massacre in 1890.

records.text: At the end of the American Civil War in 1865, the 13th Amendment to the American Constitution abolished slavery.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.section: Civil rights movement in the United States (1954–1968)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 34

records.text: Despite the abolition of slavery, Jim Crow Laws in the Southern States legally enforced racial segregation and inequality, protecting the interests of the white majority and restricting the rights of African Americans, including their right to vote. Different groups formed to overturn these laws (e.g. the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC)).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.section: Civil rights movement in the United States (1954–1968)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 34

records.text: Leaders such as Dr Martin Luther King Jr. were pivotal during this time, but change was due to the collective advocacy of thousands of everyday men, women, and children.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.section: Civil rights movement in the United States (1954–1968)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 34

records.text: Activists used a range of strategies to achieve civil rights for African Americans in the South. These included non-violent protests such as sit-ins (e.g. Greensboro), boycotts (e.g. Montgomery Bus Boycott), and legal challenges (e.g. Brown vs Board of Education). Young people were at the forefront of many campaigns (e.g. the Birmingham Campaign, Little Rock Nine).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.section: Civil rights movement in the United States (1954–1968)
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 34

records.text: The 1964 Civil Rights Act and the 1965 Voting Rights Act were the highpoints of the movement.

records.text: Natural processes interact with human activities to create environmental impacts that affect people.

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 35

records.text: Note: The two prescribed illustrative examples are floods and earthquakes; however, teachers in areas affected by natural hazards may choose to replace one of these with volcanoes, tsunami, or landslides if it better reflects the experiences of students in their class.

records.text: Natural processes affect landforms and become hazards when they pose a risk to life or property.

records.text: ‘The four Rs’ (Reduction, Readiness, Response, Recovery) underpin the emergency management system in New Zealand.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 35

records.text: Consequences for people affected by natural disasters include loss of life, loss of property and marae, damage to urupā (burial grounds), damage to infrastructure, siltation, damage to transport links, disruption to lives and livelihoods, psychological, and long- term health impacts. (See Science Year 10: Plate tectonics)

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 35

records.text: River systems comprise a source, tributaries, channel, and mouth. Rivers vary from fast-flowing mountain, to braided (e.g. Rakaia River) and meandering (e.g. Waikato River).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 35

records.text: In te ao Māori, rivers are living ancestors with their own mauri (life force), which carries an obligation to care for the whole river system** (e.g. the Whanganui River | Te Awa Tupua was recognised in 2017 as an indivisible, living whole and is represented by appointed guardians from the Crown and local iwi who act on its behalf to uphold its health and well-being).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 35

records.text: Many towns and cities in New Zealand are located on river floodplains, which are the lower, flatter reaches of rivers.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 35

records.text: Topographical maps use contour lines to show the height of the land above sea level. The wider apart the contour lines, the flatter the land. Grid references are used to locate specific points.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 35

records.text: Flooding occurs due to amount and duration of rainfall and storms and their impacts on river systems and urban areas.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 35

records.text: Climate change can impact the severity of floods. The increase in greenhouse gases from the burning of fossil fuels warms the atmosphere. A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, which generates heavier rainfall and more intense storms resulting in increased surface runoff and greater flood risk.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 35

records.text: Human activities within the river system (e.g. deforestation, slash management of forests, building and farming on flood-prone land) can magnify the impact of flooding.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 35

records.text: Urban areas have many impermeable surfaces such as concrete, asphalt, and buildings. These stop water soaking into the ground and can contribute to flooding.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 36

records.text: Flooding risks are managed through weather forecasting, river level warnings, stopbanks, river diversions, the creation of more permeable surfaces, and the clearing of drains and gutters.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 36

records.text: People protect themselves by having emergency kits, evacuating, and moving to higher ground when needed.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 36

records.text: New Zealand’s location on the Pacific Ring of Fire makes the country vulnerable to earthquakes.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 36

records.text: Earthquakes occur through tectonic plate movement, and the physical consequence of earthquakes includes ground vibration, rupture, uplift, subsidence, liquefaction, and tsunami.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 36

records.text: Many cultures had stories to explain earthquakes (e.g. Poseidon for the Ancient Greeks, Neptune for the Ancient Romans, Namazu in Japan). In te ao Māori the legend of Rūaumoko is a traditional Māori explanation for earthquakes.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 36

records.text: Earthquakes are unpredictable but are managed through monitoring and planning by Earth Sciences New Zealand.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 36

records.text: Personal safety responses include ‘Drop, Cover, and Hold’, and ‘Long or Strong, Get Gone’ strategies, keeping emergency kits ready, and knowing evacuation routes for tsunamis.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 36

records.text: The ability of a community to manage hazards is influenced by accessibility, costs, and available resources, and how they come together to support each other.**
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 36

records.text: Short-term responses include search and rescue, marae as a focal point for support, response and recovery, provision of essentials, temporary fixes, financial aid, and humanitarian assistance and citizen-initiated volunteering.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 36

records.text: Longer-term responses include reconstruction and mitigation but may also include relocation.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 36

records.text: Consumer rights are the laws and protections people are entitled to when buying goods and services within New Zealand, such as: accurate information o fit for purpose goods o remedies if something goes wrong. o

records.section: Financial systems / Consumer rights and responsibilities
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 37

records.text: Consumer responsibilities are the obligations on the other side of that relationship, such as: reading agreements o using a product as intended o checking the reliability of the seller. o

records.text: Advertising can have a direct or subconscious influence on spending such as social media, influencers, online and physical advertisements, and branding.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 37

records.text: Some in-person and online businesses use tactics such as fake urgency, hidden costs, and pre-ticked add-ons to influence decisions instead of helping people choose.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 37

records.text: Different ways of paying (e.g. cash, debit cards, credit cards) each have advantages and disadvantages.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 37

records.text: When borrowing money, you usually pay interest. This means you may repay much more than the original cost.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 37

records.text: Credit is the ability to borrow money. It allows you to access money you do not currently have (e.g. a credit card).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 37

records.text: Debt is the amount of money you owe. It must be paid back, usually in set amounts and at set times (e.g. money owed on a credit card, loans, mortgages, or buy now, pay later).

records.text: Representative democracy shapes how people can participate and influence political decisions.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 40

records.text: New Zealand is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system of government. This means that our head of state is a sovereign. The King is represented in New Zealand by the Governor-General.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 40

records.text: New Zealand’s parliamentary, representative democracy differs from other systems of government, such as direct democracies (e.g. Switzerland), presidential systems (e.g. USA), federal systems (e.g. Australia), and autocracies (e.g. North Korea). Constitutional monarchies themselves vary in how much power a monarch keeps. In New Zealand, the monarch’s role is ceremonial, and the government is run by elected ministers. In Tonga, reforms in 2010 introduced a mostly elected legislature, but the king still appoints the prime minister, the cabinet, and judges.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 40

records.text: New Zealand is a constitutional monarchy, modelled on the British Westminster parliament where the power of the King or Queen of the nation is limited by the constitution.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 40

records.text: New Zealand’s Constitution sets out rules about what government can or cannot do with its power. It is not written in one law; it is many laws and customs that make up the constitution, including te Tiriti o Waitangi / the Treaty of Waitangi, the Constitution Act, and the Bill of Rights.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 40

records.text: Te Tiriti o Waitangi / The Treaty of Waitangi are founding constitutional documents with three articles addressing Crown governance, Māori rights to land, resources, taonga (something of value), and equal protections for all.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 40

records.text: The two texts use different key terms (kāwanatanga, sovereignty, tino rangatiratanga, taonga) leading to ongoing debate about what was agreed.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 40

records.text: The Court of Appeal in 1987 (Sir Robin Cooke) concluded that the Treaty created a foundational partnership between Crown and Māori. (See History Year 8 New Zealand History: Key Features of te Tiriti o Waitangi / the Treaty of Waitangi)
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 40

records.text: The New Zealand Constitution is flexible. MPs can change most of it by simply voting. This is different from countries like the United States, where the constitution is very hard to change.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 40

records.text: Every three years, people 18 years and older get two votes under the Mixed Member Proportional voting system (MMP): one for a person to become a MP for a local area (electorate), and one for a party (party vote) to represent them in Parliament and make decisions on things they care about.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 40

records.text: People of Māori descent can choose to put their name on the Māori roll instead and vote for someone to represent a Māori electorate; the second vote is for the party they want to govern the country.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 41

records.text: Parties with the most votes get the most seats in Parliament and can form a government. Often two or more parties need to make agreements or coalitions to get enough seats to be the government.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 41

records.text: The leader of the biggest party in a government coalition usually becomes Prime Minister. This is different from other democracies, for example, that vote directly for a President.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 41

records.text: New Zealand has three branches of government: the Legislative Branch is made up of the MPs who scrutinise o and vote on laws, and the Governor-General, who represents the Sovereign (King or Queen) of New Zealand and agrees to these laws the Executive branch is made up of senior MPs from the o governing party/parties; they meet as a Cabinet (a committee of Ministers) each week to decide policy and suggest laws and are supported by the public service the Judiciary is the third branch; it is made up of all the judges o of New Zealand, who explain what different laws and rights mean and make sure these are followed.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 41

records.text: Having different roles and responsibilities for each branch of government aims to stop any one branch having too much power.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 41

records.text: In New Zealand, the media has an important role to ask questions of government, explain what is happening to the public, share people’s concerns, and is subject to critique itself to ensure trustworthy reporting. Because of this, it is sometimes called the fourth ‘estate’ or branch. Ensuring the news is reliable and trustworthy is important for all members of a democracy.

records.text: Citizens can be involved in parliamentary law-making by talking to local MPs, petitioning for law changes, or writing and presenting submissions about draft law.

records.text: Not all campaigns achieve their intended outcome. For example, the 2015–16 New Zealand flag referendum involved a nationwide campaign to consider changing the national flag, but voters ultimately chose to retain the existing flag.

records.text: Who gets a vote in a democracy has been contested for over 2,000 years. Throughout history, diverse groups have campaigned for the right to vote. More recently, this has included advocacy for 16-year-olds such as Make It 16.

records.text: As settlers demanded more land and gained power through colonial government systems, Māori became excluded and tensions increased because of competing economic interests, cultural beliefs, and ideas about control.

records.section: New Zealand history / Causes of the New Zealand Wars

records.text: Governors such as Gore Browne were concerned about the settler pressure for land, but he was also determined that Crown authority would prevail when it came to what he saw as challenges from the Kiingitanga. Meanwhile, the Colonial Office in London urged restraint as it did not want the financial burden of war. Some iwi also supported the Crown in its wars, or were neutral. This might be because the Crown was fighting a traditional enemy, or the iwi were in close proximity to settler populations and needed to be careful.

records.text: Māori worked to protect their whenua (land), mana, and tino rangatiratanga (self-determination) as colonial pressure increased, forming movements like the Kiingitanga to unite iwi and maintain authority over land and people.

records.text: Polynesian navigators settled islands across the Pacific, including the Cook Islands, Tonga, Niue, Sāmoa, and New Zealand, using stars, ocean currents, winds, and bird migrations to guide their voyages. records.text: New Zealand politicians saw the Pacific as important for defence, trade, and regional influence and sought a greater role in Pacific affairs.

records.text: In 2002, New Zealand formally apologised to Sāmoa for aspects of its colonial administration, including its handling of the influenza epidemic and actions against the Mau Movement.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: Pacific peoples maintained their languages, identities, cultural traditions, and family connections throughout the colonial period.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: In Sāmoa, the Mau Movement used peaceful protest to oppose New Zealand rule and demand independence.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: Sāmoa achieved independence in 1962, the Cook Islands became self-governing in free association with New Zealand in 1965, with Niue following in 1974.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: Some Pacific nations later adopted new or Indigenous names, including Kiribati (Gilbert Islands), Vanuatu (New Hebrides), and Sāmoa (Western Sāmoa), as part of strengthening cultural identity and self-determination.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: Despite self-government, the Cook Islands, Niue, and Sāmoa maintained strong constitutional, cultural, family, and economic links with New Zealand.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: Tonga is the only Pacific Island nation that was never formally colonised. In the mid-1800s, King George Tupou I united the kingdom, strengthening its stability, sovereignty, and independence.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: In 1839, King Tupou I dedicated Tonga to God through Tukufonua ki Langi, an event that shaped the nation’s Christian identity and is remembered by many Tongans as an affirmation of Tonga’s sovereignty and independence.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: Although Tonga was a British Protected State from 1900 to 1970, it retained its Indigenous monarchy and self-governance. Following the end of the protectorate, Tonga continued as an independent constitutional monarchy.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: Migration from the Cook Islands, Niue, Tonga, and Sāmoa strengthened family, cultural, and economic connections with New Zealand during the 20th century.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: Pacific peoples have made significant contributions to New Zealand’s communities, language, arts, sport, politics, and economy. (See Geography Year 7: International Migration)
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: During the 1970s, Pacific peoples were disproportionately targeted through discriminatory immigration enforcement, causing lasting harm. In 2021, the New Zealand government formally apologised for the Dawn Raids and acknowledged the injustices experienced by Pacific communities.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: People from the Cook Islands, Niue, Tonga, Sāmoa, and New Zealand may interpret shared historical events differently because of their experiences and cultural perspectives.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: Pacific oral histories, family stories, cultural traditions, and written records all contribute to our understanding of the past.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: Considering multiple perspectives helps build a fuller understanding of New Zealand’s shared history with Pacific peoples and its continuing significance today.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 45

records.text: India was part of the British Empire from 1757 to 1947, and under direct rule by Britain from 1858 (the British Raj).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.section: Gandhi and the campaign for Indian Independence (1915–
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 46

records.text: Many Indian people wanted independence because Britain exploited India’s natural resources (e.g. cotton, tea, minerals) and treated Indian people as second class citizens (e.g. excluded them from positions of power and discriminated against them).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.section: Gandhi and the campaign for Indian Independence (1915–
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 46

records.text: British rule affected people in India differently depending on their social position, religion, gender, region, and circumstances, resulting in a range of experiences and perspectives. For example: some wealthy members of society gained education, o employment, and political opportunities under British administration, while others (e.g. many farmers and workers) faced poverty, high taxes, and limited political rights railway construction improved communications and trade, but o mainly served British interests, displaced some traditional workers, and left many rural communities with fewer benefits than cities.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.section: Gandhi and the campaign for Indian Independence (1915–
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 46

records.text: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, commonly known as Mahatma Gandhi, became the leading figure of the Indian National Congress and introduced the idea of Satyagraha (peaceful resistance) to achieve independence.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 46

records.text: Gandhi and the Independence Movement used civil disobedience and non-cooperation tactics. These tactics included protests (e.g. the Salt March 1930), boycotting of British goods, and a refusal to cooperate with British authorities.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 46

records.text: Indian people responded to British colonial rule in different ways, including peaceful protest, political activism, local community organising, and calls for self-government and independence. For example, some cooperated with British authorities through government or military service, while others supported the Indian National Congress and Gandhi's peaceful protest campaigns, including the Salt March. Some groups favoured more radical methods, including armed resistance, to achieve independence.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 46

records.text: Although Gandhi was the figurehead of the Independence Movement, many others, including local leaders, women, workers, students, and community organisations, contributed to the movement and helped mobilise millions of Indians.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 46

records.text: India gained independence in 1947 after decades of campaigning, protest, political activism, and negotiation. The country was divided into two sovereign nations – India and Pakistan.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 46

records.text: Partition led to large-scale migration, violence, and displacement. For example, many Hindus and Sikhs moved from areas that became Pakistan to India, while many Muslims moved from India to Pakistan. These migrations involved millions of people, and continue to shape identities, family histories, and relations between India and Pakistan today.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 46

records.text: People in India, Britain, Pakistan, and elsewhere may interpret the causes, significance, and outcomes of Indian independence differently because of their experiences, identities, and historical perspectives.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 47

records.text: The rapid growth of tourism impacts on the sustainability of vulnerable human and physical environments.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 48

records.text: Tourism can be domestic and international, and can be inbound and outbound.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 48

records.text: Tourism is generally for a short term, ranging from days through to months.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 48

records.text: People travel as tourists for recreation and relaxation, adventure, cultural and heritage experiences, health/medical, education, pilgrimages, and visiting friends and family.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 48

records.text: Flow maps show quantity and direction of tourist travel using arrows. The pattern of tourism varies by country, seasons, and high and low seasons.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 48

records.text: Tourism has a long history in New Zealand (e.g. the ‘wonder country’ tours in the 19th century).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 48

records.text: New Zealand is an attractive tourist destination because of the unique natural environments and opportunities to experience iconic destinations, tours, adventure activities, and film locations.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 48

records.text: Māori have always played a central role in New Zealand tourism through cultural experiences, guiding, and ecotourism that connects tourists to the land. Māori have also played a role in establishing New Zealand on the global stage (e.g. kapa haka groups, Te Māori exhibition 1984).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 48

records.text: Tourism is a large export earner for New Zealand and a major global business; it generates employment and revenue, supports regional development, and showcases cultures.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 48

records.text: Tourism can also place pressure on sensitive ecosystems, infrastructure (e.g. water supply, sewage systems, road congestion), increased cost of local housing, and resident dissatisfaction caused by noise and crowds.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 48

records.text: Communities and government use a range of ways to manage the pressures of growth (e.g. restricting or closing sensitive sites, controlling short-term rentals, visitor levies). Tourism sustainability initiatives need to balance economic growth, environmental protection, and cultural preservation.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 48

records.text: Pacific Island nations attract tourists through a combination of the uniqueness of the natural environments and cultures.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: While tourism is a major source of foreign exchange and revenue, and provides jobs and preserves cultural traditions, it also changes the character, culture, and landscape of places.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: The heavy reliance on coastal-based tourism makes Pacific nations economically vulnerable to the impacts of climate change through sea-level rise and greater storm intensity and damage.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: Overtourism also places pressure on the environment and local resources. Many Pacific nations have policy interventions to manage this (e.g. French Polynesia has banned cruise ships carrying more than 3,500 passengers, Palau has shifted to low- impact tourism, Pacific Tourism Organisation is working towards eliminating single-use plastics).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: The interactions between natural processes at the coast and people’s activities creates sustainability challenges that need to be actively managed.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: Waves erode the coast through hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution (corrosion).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: Transportation involves the movement of material along the coast by longshore drift.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: Deposition occurs when wave energy is too low to carry material.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: Erosional landforms include headlands, bays, caves, arches, stacks, stumps, and wave-cut platforms.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: Depositional landforms include beaches, spits, and sand dunes.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: Human activity (e.g. building near or on the coast, vegetation removal, trampling of dunes, vehicles on beaches, sand mining, seawalls, or dams on rivers) can disrupt natural processes (e.g. disrupt the natural sand budget).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: Human activities, especially burning fossil fuels (e.g. coal, oil, and gas), add greenhouse gases to the atmosphere. These gases trap more heat around Earth, causing global temperatures to rise. This is known as global warming.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: As the planet warms, glaciers and polar ice sheets melt, adding more water to the oceans and causing sea levels to rise. The oceans also absorb most of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases. When water warms, it expands and takes up more space, which causes sea levels to rise even further.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: Define, explain, and apply concepts of natural processes, impact, and sustainability, and make connections between these concepts by exploring different contexts.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: Ask questions that explore values, ethics, bias, and consequences, including different perspectives and short- and long-term impacts. For example: Why is managed retreat such a complex issue? o What are the immediate and longer-term consequences of o coastal erosion?

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 49

records.text: Warmer oceans can make hurricanes and cyclones stronger because they provide more energy for these storms. A warmer atmosphere can also hold more water vapour, which can lead to heavier rainfall and a greater risk of flooding.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 50

records.text: Raised sea levels and increased intensity of storms makes coastal areas more vulnerable to flooding (inundation). High-energy storm waves can also severely erode cliffs, causing cliff collapse and remove large quantities of sand and dunes in a short time.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 50

records.text: The impacts of coastal processes can be seen using GIS comparing with historical maps or photographs, data from satellite imagery, and aerial photographs. GIS links locational data to other descriptive information to show patterns, relationships, and changes over time.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 50

records.text: Coastal risks associated with environmental change can be addressed using: hard engineering methods such as sea walls, groynes, and o rock armour soft engineering methods such as beach nourishment and dune o restoration and planting.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 50

records.text: Moving people away from the coast (managed retreat) allows natural coastal processes to continue, but relocation is complex and contested.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 50

records.text: Decisions about managing environmental change at the coast are influenced by economic, social, and environmental factors.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 50

records.text: There are multiple and sometimes competing perspectives (e.g. property owners, ratepayers, insurers, councils and central government, hapū and iwi) on managing coastal erosion and inundation.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 50

records.text: Explaining how environments change through natural processes, and how people’s activities can be in conflict in coastal areas.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 50

records.text: Explaining how a coastal management plan seeks to sustain both natural processes and human activity.

records.text: The economy is the system of how money, goods, and services move between people, businesses, and governments around the world.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 51

records.text: The economy is made up of different sectors; primary (raw materials), secondary (manufacturing), and tertiary (services), with volunteering making an important non-financial contribution.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 51

records.text: The Māori economy is closely linked to rangatiratanga (self- determination) and plays a growing role in New Zealand’s prosperity. Treaty settlements have enabled some iwi to build asset bases, which they have used for commercial and social investment. New Zealand relies heavily on exporting primary products such as dairy and providing tertiary services such as tourism. New Zealand also imports goods from other countries (e.g. cars from Japan).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 51

records.text: Global and local prices are shaped by two primary economic forces: supply – how much of something is available o demand – how much people want or need it. o

records.text: Inflation is the general increase in prices over time, which means money buys less than it did before. Inflation affects the cost of living, savings, and income.

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 51

records.text: Global markets are the systems through which countries buy and sell goods, services, and resources with each other. The prices of everyday goods like petrol and food are often shaped by what is happening in global markets, not just locally.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 51

records.text: People, groups, and businesses can invest in global markets, which means their savings and investments can be affected by what happens economically around the world.

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 51

records.text: Changes in the economy (e.g. growth and downturns) affect prices, wages, and employment, which in turn impact financial decisions.

records.text: Being involved in global markets means that events in other countries can affect the cost of living, jobs, and financial choices at home.

records.text: During World War Two, Nazi policies developed into the systematic murder of millions of people including 6 million Jewish people.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 45

records.text: At the Evian Conference (1938) New Zealand expressed sympathy for Jewish refugees.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.section: New Zealand’s mixed response to Jewish refugees
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 45

records.text: The government also condemned the November Pogroms (1938) (Kristallnacht) but remained extremely reluctant to accept refugees fleeing Nazi Germany.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.section: New Zealand’s mixed response to Jewish refugees
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 45

records.text: Immigration restrictions were tightened, and it was only after pressure from Britain that New Zealand agreed to admit approximately 1,000 refugees.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.section: New Zealand’s mixed response to Jewish refugees
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 45

records.text: The experiences of the Holocaust remind us to be aware of how hatred towards other groups can lead to terrible consequences. There have been other genocides committed since the Holocaust (e.g. Rwanda, Cambodia, Srebrenica).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 45

records.text: Healthy democracies strive to preserve safeguards against authoritarianism (e.g. separation of powers, free and fair elections, rule of law, independent judiciary, free media and human rights protections). (See also Civics and Society Year 8: Democratic Values) OR
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 45

records.text: British rule over Ireland began as early as the 12th century, but many Irish people continued to believe that Ireland should have more control over its own government, while retaining its own Irish language and culture (e.g. traditional sports, local arts). However, some people, particularly many Protestants in Ulster, supported remaining part of the United Kingdom.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 45

records.text: Periodic rebellions from the 17th century contributed to the development of nationalist movements such as the Fenians/Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB), the Irish Volunteers, and Sinn Féin, which sought greater Irish self-governance or independence. These movements played an important role in the 1916 Easter Rising, a key turning point in Irish politics.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 45

records.text: Although the Rising was defeated and Irish opinion remained divided, Britain's harsh response, including the execution of many of the Rising's leaders, increased support for Irish independence.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 45

records.text: Leaders such as Michael Collins and Éamon de Valera, along with many ordinary Irish men and women, continued working to challenge British control.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 45

records.text: Victorious in the 1918 election in Ireland, Sinn Féin refused to take seats in the British Parliament and instead established Dáil Éireann, which declared Irish independence in 1919. Britain rejected this declaration.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 45

records.text: During the resulting Irish War of Independence (1919–1921), Irish republicans and British forces fought a guerrilla war until eventually a negotiated settlement was reached.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 46

records.text: As a result of the conflict, in 1922 most of Ireland became the Irish Free State and gained substantial self-government within the British Commonwealth.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 46

records.text: Six counties in the north chose to remain part of the United Kingdom and became known as Northern Ireland.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 46

records.text: The movement changed Ireland's political system and demonstrated how individuals and groups can challenge existing power structures to affect political change.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 46

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 51

records.text: Governments also have income. This is generated from taxation, state-owned enterprises (government-owned businesses) and investment.

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 51

records.text: The democratic system allows people to vote for policies that represent their individual, local, and national economic priorities.

records.text: Taxation is money the government collects through various means to fund public services (e.g. schools and hospitals), infrastructure (e.g. roads and public transport), social support (e.g. pensions and benefits), and to influence behaviour (e.g. taxes on tobacco, alcohol or pollution).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 51

records.text: Tax is collected from income (e.g. PAYE) and spending (e.g. GST).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 51

records.text: People pay different amounts in income tax based on what they earn.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 51

records.text: Rates are local taxes paid by property owners and businesses, based on the value and use of their land and buildings.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 51

records.text: Local councils use rates to fund services such as water, sewage, libraries, parks, and local infrastructure.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 51

records.text: Evading tax is illegal and reduces funding available for public services.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 51

records.text: Some types of employment contracts are casual, part-time, full- time, or fixed term, and they have different effects on entitlements, and income security.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 52

records.text: Important clauses to understand relate to wages, hours, leave, flexible working, notice periods, and trial periods.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 52

records.text: Saving helps keep money safe but is a slower way to grow your money.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 52

records.text: Different savings options have different features such as fees, interest rates, and withdrawal rules.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 52

records.text: There are different types of investments, and each has different risks and possible returns.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 52

records.text: Investment decisions are influenced by: values and beliefs (e.g. sustainable investment, local o investment) attitude towards risk o personal circumstances, including when people need their o money back, how much they can invest, and whether they spread their money across different investments.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 52

records.text: When making the decision to take on debt, consider: the reason for borrowing (e.g. an immediate purchase or o investment in your future) who is providing the credit (e.g. reliability and trustworthiness, o rate of interest) manageability and impact (e.g. how long it will take to pay off, o whether you can afford to pay it off, or whether it will lead to further debt).
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 52

records.text: Credit cards and loans both charge interest, but compound interest means the amount owed can grow quickly over time, affecting financial burdens significantly.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 52

records.text: Financial tools from reliable and impartial providers can help with managing your money and making financial decisions.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.section: Managing money / Tools and advice for money management
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 52

records.text: Financial advice can help with money management and assist informed financial decision-making around budgeting, saving, debt, borrowing, KiwiSaver, investing, insurance, and planning for the future. (See Mathematics and Statistics Year 9–10: Number, Financial Mathematics)
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.section: Managing money / Tools and advice for money management
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 52

records.text: People or groups can access financial advice from places such as financial advisers, mentors, coaches, banks, budgeting services, mortgage and insurance brokers, investment providers and advisers, and community organisations.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.section: Managing money / Tools and advice for money management
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 52

records.text: The purpose of pensions and retirement savings is to provide an income during retirement. Superannuation is a government payment made to people after they reach a certain age.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 53

records.text: The sustainability of superannuation schemes is often debated, with governments considering options such as changing the age of eligibility, who qualifies, and how payments are adjusted over time.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 53

records.text: KiwiSaver is a voluntary savings scheme to help New Zealand residents prepare for retirement. Different contribution fund types offer varying risk and return. Starting KiwiSaver contributions early increases the return through compounding returns.
records.subject: Social Sciences
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 53

records.text: Visual arts elements, principles, and conventions are used in artworks to communicate ideas and express personal stories, values, and worldviews. These may include symbolic forms and patterns that carry significance, responsibilities, and protocols.
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 7, page 26

records.text: Visual art conventions are characteristics and constraints specific to different fields of art (e.g. design, painting, sculpture, photography, digital image-making and editing, printmaking, toi Māori practices such as raranga (weaving) and whakairo (carving)).
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 7, page 26

records.text: Artists use conventions to communicate ideas and draw on cultural traditions for inspiration.
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 7, page 26

records.text: Composition principles are applied to arrange visual elements in ways that communicate ideas and guide the viewer’s response: visual hierarchy: the organisation of elements to show importance or guide viewer attention o emphasis: the creation of a focal point in the artwork to highlight the most important area or idea. o
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 7, page 26

records.text: Artists use observational drawing to accurately represent objects and forms.
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 7, page 26

records.text: Artmaking is a developmental and reflective process that involves generating, exploring, developing, and resolving ideas. Artists select conventions and make purposeful decisions to develop work and shape meaning.
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 7, page 26

records.text: Artworks are shaped by cultural and community knowledge, including Indigenous knowledge passed intergenerationally. They embody values, belonging, and connection, and carry responsibilities and meanings.
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 7, page 26

records.text: Compositions are created for specific purposes. (e.g. in toi Māori whakapapa is communicated through whakairo (carvings) on the wharenui, Mexican murals represent historic events, Dutch and Flemish portraits honour notable people).
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 7, page 26

records.text: Artists purposefully select materials, tools, and techniques (e.g. blending, carving, digital methods) to shape meaning and expression and to create effects.
records.subject: Visual Arts

records.text: Artmaking materials, tools, and techniques (e.g. chisels, craft knives, scribes) require safe practice.
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 7, page 26

records.text: Artworks are created, shared, and experienced in different ways and settings (e.g. galleries, community spaces).
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 7, page 26

records.text: Artworks can be interpreted using art terminology, including language, symbols, and text, to describe meaning, intent, and context.
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 7, page 26

records.text: Symbols, patterns, and practices in art express values and worldviews. Observation and responding to artworks deepen understanding of their significance.
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 7, page 26

records.text: Exploration of art history helps us recognise artists, movements, and influences. Artworks from different times and places show the ideas, materials, and styles of their era.
records.subject: Visual Arts

records.text: Combine visual arts elements, principles, and conventions to express identities, stories, and worldviews by purposefully selecting processes, materials, and techniques (e.g. blending, carving, digital methods) to communicate meaning.

records.text: Techniques (e.g. voice, body, movement, space), conventions (e.g. narration, flashback, split stage, tableau), and technologies (e.g. costume, props, lighting) are the three components used to construct drama. They are selected to shape meaning and influence how ideas, situations, and relationships are understood.
records.subject: Drama
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 23

records.text: Drama components are selected and combined to shape meaning and influence how ideas, situations, and relationships are understood.
records.subject: Drama
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 23

records.text: Improvisation (making things up on the spot without prior planning) is a tool actors use to generate ideas, explore characters and situations, test possibilities, and respond quickly during performance. Accepting others’ ideas and building on their offers is essential to sustaining improvisation.
records.subject: Drama
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 23

records.text: As ideas are refined and expanded, improvisation can develop into devised drama, generating original work through collaboration, experimentation, discussion, and shared decision-making.
records.subject: Drama
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 23

records.text: Script conventions (e.g. character lists, dialogue, stage directions, scene, and act divisions) are used to support actors to: explore character, situation, meaning, and different interpretations o structure the action and guide performance. o
records.subject: Drama
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 23

records.text: Playwrights make decisions regarding the objective, relationships, status, and context of the characters in a drama.
records.subject: Drama
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 23

records.text: Sequencing, tension, and pacing are tools used to shape work with intention to communicate ideas to an audience.
records.subject: Drama
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 23

records.text: Technologies (e.g. props, costume, sound, lighting) support character, place, and mood.
records.subject: Drama
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 23

records.text: Drama enriches societies around the world by providing opportunities to examine relationships, culture, identity, and social issues through performance and storytelling.
records.subject: Drama
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 23

records.text: Care, trust, and respect, alongside working together with a shared purpose, expressed in te ao Māori as manaakitanga and mahi ngātahi, enable participants to negotiate ideas, make collective decisions, and sustain collaborative creative processes.
records.subject: Drama
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 23

records.text: Techniques, conventions, and technologies can be combined to communicate meaning in drama.
records.subject: Drama
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 23

records.text: Dramatic choices shape how an audience understands ideas, characters, relationships, and situations (e.g. use of melodrama to explore relationships, mime to convey emotions).
records.subject: Drama
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 8, page 23

records.text: Context, perspective, and audience all shape how the same piece of drama can be interpreted differently by different people.

records.text: Observing and responding to drama builds understanding of its intention (what is being communicated), process (how it was created), and meaning (what it represents).

records.text: Visual arts elements, principles, and conventions are used in artworks to communicate ideas and express personal stories, values, and worldviews. These may include symbolic forms and patterns that carry significance, responsibilities, and protocols.

records.text: Visual art conventions are characteristics and constraints specific to different fields of art (e.g. design, painting, sculpture, photography, digital image-making and editing, printmaking, toi Māori practices such as raranga (weaving) and whakairo (carving)).

records.text: Music from different historical eras, styles, and genres has unique features and stylistic conventions (e.g. Medieval: chant, Renaissance: harmony, Baroque: ornamentation, Classical: balance, Romantic: expression, Modern: innovation, singer- songwriter: storytelling, musical theatre: narrative, Pacific music: rhythm, fusion genres: blending).

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 32

records.text: Music shows how traditions and innovations interact across cultures and time (e.g. taonga puoro (Māori instruments) in film, Polynesian, Hip Hop, digital, traditional sound sources).

records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 32

records.text: Performers (e.g. as seen in Polyfest, Te Matatini, and The Big Sing) use a variety of techniques in ensembles to support balance, blend and cohesion, including non-verbal communication (e.g. shared breath, eye contact), placement of performers, and levels of amplification.

records.text: Performance practices and protocols differ across genres and cultures (e.g. rock performance, gospel, orchestra, tikanga and kawa in Māori contexts).

records.text: Musicians select and apply forms of music notation and literacy appropriate to the style, context, and purpose of the music, using systems such as oral/aural transmission, notation, chord charts, lead sheets, tablature (TAB), DAW-based notation, graphic notation, looping, recording, and collaborative songwriting to shape, refine, and communicate musical ideas.
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 32

records.text: Dotted notes (e.g. dotted whole notes, dotted half notes, dotted quarter notes) extend a note’s duration by adding half its original value.

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 32

records.text: In simple time (2/4, 3/4, 4/4) quavers and semiquavers are beamed together to clearly define individual, divisible beats (e.g. beamed in 2s and 4s).
records.subject: Music

records.text: On the bass stave, two ledger lines above the stave is E and two ledger lines below is C.

records.text: A key signature indicates the set of sharps or flats used throughout a piece of music to define its key: C major: no sharps or flats o F major: one flat (B ) o ♭ G major: one sharp (F♯). o
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 33

records.text: Articulation refers to the way individual notes are started, sustained, connected, and ended: legato means notes are performed smoothly o staccato means notes are performed detached. o
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 33

records.text: Tempo terms describe the speed of the music: adagio is a slow tempo o andante is a relaxed walking pace o moderato is a moderate pace o allegro is a fast pace o presto is a very fast pace. o
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 33

records.text: Taonga puoro (Māori instruments) often feature as solo instruments, using their unique sounds to mimic the human voice and share traditional stories (pūrākau).
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 33

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 33

records.text: Texture can change throughout a piece of music or can remain constant.

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 33

records.text: A motif is a short, distinct melodic or rhythmic musical idea that is repeated, transformed, and developed throughout a piece of music to drive the structure and thematic narrative.
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 33

records.text: Chords can be represented by a range of symbols. Two of the main symbols are Roman numeral and chord symbols.
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 33

records.text: Major chords consist of a root, major third, and perfect fifth: C major: C-E-G o F major: F-A-C o G major: G-B-D. o
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 33

records.text: A minor chord consists of a root, minor third, and perfect fifth: A minor: A-C-E o D minor: D-F-A o
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 33

records.text: E minor: E-G-B. o
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 34

records.text: A lowercase Roman numeral indicates a minor chord.
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 34

records.text: It is important to consider the key signature of the scale when building chords and triads.
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 34

records.text: The tonic chord (Chord I) is a triad built on the tonic (1st note of the scale) (I in major, i in minor).
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 34

records.text: The dominant chord (Chord V) is a triad built on the dominant (5th note of the scale) (V in major, v in minor).
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 34

records.text: The dominant chord typically resolves to the tonic chord to create a finished sound.
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 34

records.text: The subdominant chord (Chord IV) is a triad built on the fourth (4th note of the scale) (IV in major, iv in minor).
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 34

records.text: The bass line is the series of the lowest notes in a composition. It outlines the harmony of a section.
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 34

records.text: A digital audio workstation (DAW) is a linear, time-based environment for recording, sequencing, arranging, and producing sound. It uses a timeline to organise audio and MIDI data, with track headers and transport controls (e.g. play, record, loop) enabling navigation, playback, recording, and arrangement.
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 34

records.text: The digital grid of a DAW is organised according to musical time (e.g. time signatures such as 4/4). MIDI data can be edited in piano-roll views and used to control virtual instruments (VSTs), while audio data represents recorded sound.
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 34

records.text: Digital signal flow follows a basic signal path from microphone or instrument → audio interface → DAW → monitors/headphones.
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 34

records.text: Notation software is a document-based environment for music literacy, composition, and publication. It represents musical ideas using standard notation (e.g. staff/stave, notes, rests) intended for performance by musicians.
records.subject: Music
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 34

records.text: Distinguish the difference between recorded audio sounds (e.g. vocals, guitar) and electronically generated sounds (e.g. synthesisers, MIDI instruments) in a track.
records.subject: Music

records.text: Identify which notes, symbols, or regions in a notation score or DAW timeline correspond to the sounds being heard.

records.text: Visual arts processes (e.g. planning, developing, refining), materials (e.g. paint, clay, ink), techniques (e.g. blending, carving, layering, digital printing), elements (e.g. line, colour, texture, space, form, tone), and principles shape creative intention.
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 35

records.text: Visual arts principles, built on from previous knowledge, include: perspective: creating depth to show how objects appear o smaller when farther away rule of thirds and alignment: arranging elements so they line o up visually and feel balanced extended colour theory (e.g. harmonious, complementary, o tertiary colours).
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 35

records.text: There are specific conventions associated with different artforms and practices. These include: design: layout, typography, visual hierarchy, balance, o contrast painting: brushwork, layering, colour blending, composition, o perspective photography: framing, depth of field, lighting, focus, viewpoint o printmaking: repetition, pattern, carving, positive/negative o space, texture, mark-making o sculpture: form, balance, space, material, surface treatment.
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 35

records.text: Visual arts processes, materials, and techniques have differences and commonalities across different cultures and practices.

records.text: Elements of artforms often carry symbolic meaning and use specific practices. Indigenous artforms are grounded in cultural practices (e.g. intergenerational knowledge transmission, maintaining connections, observing cultural and ceremonial protocols, and using customary processes and materials).
records.subject: Visual Arts
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 9, page 35

records.text: Planning, reflection, and development of ideas are a part of the creative process.
