records.text: Dance can be performed in three planes: vertical, sagittal, and horizontal.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: A canon is a movement or phrase of movement that is repeated at different times by two or more dancers.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: In a simple canon, a dancer performs a movement or series of movements and then remains still while another dancer repeats the same movements. For an overlapping canon a second dancer can begin several counts behind the first dancer.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Changes of tempo can be used to create variation in a dance.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: In exact unison movement, dancers perform the same movements at the same time. Unison movement can suggest strength, unity, and harmony.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Unison movement contrasted with non-unison movement creates visual interest.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Body shapes and formations can be symmetrical or asymmetrical. Symmetry creates balance and harmony. Asymmetry creates an unbalanced and contrasting look.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Straight air pathways can suggest ideas of strength, seriousness, dignity, and purposefulness. Curved air pathways can suggest playfulness, beauty, gentleness, and uncertainty.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Body bases are how the weight of bodies is supported (e.g. standing, sitting, lying, kneeling). Some dance forms use combinations of body parts as body bases (e.g. one knee, one hand, one foot).
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Inventiveness is an important aspect of many dance styles (e.g. Hip Hop, contemporary, haka, rock and roll).
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Choreographers organise and refine movement to communicate purpose, meaning, and intention.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Dance is shaped by cultural, historical, and contemporary contexts, which influence how it is created and understood (e.g. Capoeira, Lindy Hop, Modern dance).
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Apply variations of dance elements to change movements and create a new sequence of movement.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Experiment with ways to rise and fall (e.g. collapse, melt, suspend, rise, sink, drop, stand up, push up, scramble, fall).
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Use different body parts as bases (e.g. one hand and two feet; two hands and one knee; one back, one foot, and one elbow) when creating shapes with a partner.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Experiment with tempo, long and short movements, and sudden and sustained movement.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Compose dance sequences with purposeful repetition, evaluating how it emphasises meaning.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Create sequences of movements that can be performed in unison to communicate an idea (e.g. power or strength), considering other dance elements that could strengthen the idea (e.g. straight or angular shapes).
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Use symmetry and asymmetry to create individual, paired, and group shapes. Evaluate the effects of symmetrical and asymmetrical shapes and formations in dance.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Compose group dance sequences using air pathways to convey meaning.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Create, organise, and refine choreography to communicate a clear purpose and intention.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Use rehearsal, feedback, and reflection to improve choreography and performance quality.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 28

records.text: Alignment and posture can be important for many dance styles (e.g. for safety, clarity of communication, respect for the dance style).
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Dance with other dancers uses ensemble skills (e.g. timing with others, entrances and exits, spacing, consistent focus, communication).
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Dance has been used to build community and celebration by diverse cultures throughout history.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Kapa haka can be used as a platform for iwi-specific priorities.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Folk and courtly dances differ in their origin and social purpose: Folk dances are informal, community-based expressions of o daily life that are learned informally through participation. They are performed for enjoyment. Courtly dances are very formal and are designed for those o who attend royal courts. They were created to display wealth, power, and status.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Artistic dance is created to perform for an audience. The titles of artistic dance convey ideas about the dance.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Artistic dance performed in a theatre uses theatre technologies to enhance visual interest and add to the communication of meaning.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Dance communicates meaning through choreographic choices, performance quality, and context.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Audience, purpose, and context influence how dance is interpreted and valued.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Improve posture and body positioning (e.g. knees over toes, parallel feet, hip bones facing front, shoulders back and down).
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Maintain focus throughout a performance to guide audience attention.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Dance with others to develop correct timing, spacing, group focus, and support for the communication of ideas in the dance.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Research dances performed in your community to celebrate and build a sense of belonging (e.g. Samoan Sāsā, Indian Bollywood). Learn moves from one of the dances.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Learn a folk dance (e.g. Strip the Willow, Scotland) and a courtly dance (e.g. Pavane, originally from France and England that was popular in Elizabethan times). Compare the two dances.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Invent your own version of a folk or courtly dance and as a group perform it for the class.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Analyse artistic dances: discuss the ways that the title is represented in the dance o observe how sound, lighting, and costumes communicate o ideas, moods, and feelings evaluate how choreography and performance communicate o ideas to an audience.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Use appropriate dance terminology when discussing, reflecting on, and evaluating dance works.
records.subject: Dance
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 29

records.text: Create, rehearse, and perform a dance for a specific audience.
records.subject: Dance

records.text: Drama is a collaborative art form used to communicate ideas, messages, and viewpoints.
records.subject: Drama
records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 30

records.text: Shaping improvised material into devised drama moves a piece from exploration to a structured work.

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 30

records.text: Theatre forms influence a work's style, structure, and how an audience interprets it.

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 30

records.text: Adaptation and crafting of a script, changing dialogue, structure, or action shapes how an audience understands drama.

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 30

records.text: Subtext is what a character is really thinking or feeling beneath what they say and is communicated through techniques and shaped by a character's objective.

records.text: Performance choices reveal subtext. A different selection can change how a moment is understood by an audience.

records.text: Drama explores and communicates perspectives shaped by time, place, identity, and community. records.text: Care, trust, and respect, alongside working together with a shared creative intention, expressed in te ao Māori as manaakitanga and mahi ngātahi, are essential to successful drama-making, enabling participants to co-create, solve artistic challenges, and realise shared creative purpose.

records.text: Music from different historical eras, styles, and genres has unique features and stylistic conventions (e.g. Medieval: chant, Renaissance: harmony, Baroque: ornamentation, Classical: balance, Romantic: expression, Modern: innovation, singer- songwriter: storytelling, musical theatre: narrative, Pacific music: rhythm, fusion genres: blending).

records.source: The New Zealand Curriculum — The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026, Year 10, page 32

records.text: Music shows how traditions and innovations interact across cultures and time (e.g. taonga puoro (Māori instruments) in film, Polynesian, Hip Hop, digital, traditional sound sources).

records.text: Musical innovation includes changes over time related to form, expression, instruments, and technologies (e.g. contemporary styles such as electronic music, film and game music).
